title: App requests and toolkit types
text: App Requests and Toolkits are two separate controls over what members can reach: which catalog applications a project is allowed to use, and which toolkit types exist on the deployment at all. Decide an app request A member who opens the application catalog and requests access to something their project is not configured for creates a row here — separate from the agent/skill publishing review, which is a different mechanism entirely. The queue lists pending requests with who asked and for what. Both record your decision and notify the requester in the same transaction. Approving a request records the decision and tells the requester — it does not itself grant anything. Nothing in the platform reads an approved row and automatically unlocks a capability; whether the requested application actually becomes usable depends on whether its toolkit type is enabled for that project, below. Control which toolkit types are offered Open Toolkits . This decides, per toolkit type, whether it is enabled, disabled, or restricted to named projects — always with a reason and a recorded decider. The table lists every catalogue type with its current availability and a worker support indicator. Choose enabled, disabled, or restricted; a restricted type also lists which projects can use it. A reason is required for every choice except reverting to the default. This page does not add a new toolkit type. A pre built MCP server becomes a type through Configuration's MCP Servers section, and an external provider's toolkits would arrive through Service Descriptors — a third registration path here would be a third thing to keep synchronized. The worker column is advisory: it reports whether the toolkit type is known to run on the platform's agent worker (the native Rust runtime), not whether the type is disallowed. A type the worker cannot build shows Unverified with the server's reason beside it — tracked in 865. See the toolkit catalogue for which types run.

title: Audit trail
text: Audit Trail is a read only view over what happened on the deployment — there is nothing to edit or configure here. Use it to answer "who did this, and when," whether you are investigating an incident, confirming a change actually landed, or checking whether a scheduled job ran. Review activity User events are actions a person took; System events are platform generated (for example a scheduled job firing). Each has its own tab. Narrow by date range (with quick presets like 30 minutes, today, yesterday, 7 days, or 30 days, plus an explicit From/To), event type, project, user, or errors only. A calendar style heatmap shows activity density over time, so a spike is visible before you drill into individual events. Traces and spans A second view mode, alongside events, shows execution traces and their individual spans — each row names the action and, when there is one, the tool or model that ran it. Spans can be filtered by duration band (under 10 ms, up to over 10 seconds), which is the fastest way to find what is running slowly across the deployment rather than one conversation at a time. Investigate one person From the Users page's row menu, the activity drawer filters this same audit data to one account — useful when investigating a specific person's actions rather than browsing the whole trail. See Users and roles. This page has no write path of any kind. An audit trail the product could edit would not be one. Audit Trail records what happened; it does not enforce anything. If you are looking for the controls that decide who can do what in the first place, see Users and roles.

title: Authentication
text: Authentication lives under Configuration › Authentication in the admin console. It covers how people sign in (OIDC or SAML) and how an identity provider's groups map onto project membership (SCIM). Configure an identity provider The list shows any providers already configured, one live per protocol. Choose OpenID Connect or SAML 2.0 . Issuer URL (a .well known/openid configuration URL is accepted and reduced to its issuer), Client ID, client secret, redirect URI, scopes, and whether e mail verification is required. Identity provider entity ID, SSO URL, single logout URL, and certificate(s); this service's own entity ID and ACS URL; name ID format; the e mail and name attribute mappings; whether to sign AuthnRequests; the service provider certificate; and clock skew tolerance. NameID format is a select. The values are Not requested (the default), Unspecified , Email address , Persistent and Transient . With Not requested , the identity provider sends its own default format. With Transient , the NameID changes at each sign in, so also set the e mail attribute. The service provider metadata is at https:// /auth/saml/metadata . Import it at the identity provider after you enable the provider. It is available with or without Sign authentication requests . It always contains the entity ID, the ACS URL (HTTP POST) and the selected NameID format, and it asks for signed assertions. It contains the service provider certificate only when requests are signed. Users provisioned by SCIM may sign in through this provider is off by default. Turn it on only for the provider paired with your SCIM client (for example, Entra ID's sign in app when Entra also provisions users). While it is off, a first sign in through this provider cannot take over an account that SCIM created; the sign in is refused as a conflict. A provider configured through environment variables instead of this screen uses OIDC ADOPT SCIM USERS=true for the same setting. Turning a provider on retires any other provider of the same protocol — only one live OIDC and one live SAML definition can exist at a time, because each protocol is served on one route. A stored secret is never shown in the clear — the field renders a mask, and there is no "reveal" control. To change it, enter a new value; leaving it blank keeps the existing one. Deleting a provider also deletes its stored secret, which cannot be recovered. To stop using a provider for new logins without losing its configuration, turn off "use this provider for logins" instead of deleting it. Connect an identity provider with SCIM SCIM lets an identity provider push its directory. It creates accounts when people join and deactivates them when they leave. The SCIM endpoint is /api/v2/scim/v2 . An identity provider authenticates to SCIM with a SCIM client . A SCIM client is a credential that belongs to the integration, not to a person. The audit trail records its changes as scim: . Breaking change. SCIM no longer accepts personal access tokens or browser sessions. A request with one gets 401 and the detail "SCIM requires a SCIM client credential; personal access tokens are not accepted". If your identity provider used a personal access token, create a SCIM client and replace the token in the identity provider. The panel shows the Tenant URL and the Token endpoint of this deployment, each with a copy button. You need the admin.auth.users permission to manage SCIM clients. Select New SCIM client . Type a name for the identity provider, and select a method: Secret token (Bearer) — one secret. The identity provider sends it as the bearer token on each request. OAuth2 client credentials — a client identifier and a client secret. The identity provider gets a short lived access token from the token endpoint (1 hour by default), and sends that access token. Optionally, set Expires on . The date must be from tomorrow to two years ahead. After that day the client stops working. The list shows the days left, and it shows a warning in the last 30 days. The secret shows one time only . Copy it into the identity provider before you close the dialog. Elitea keeps only a hash of the secret, so nobody can show it again. Microsoft Entra ID settings In the Entra ID enterprise application, open Provisioning , set the mode to Automatic , and use these values: | Entra ID field | Bearer authentication | OAuth2 client credentials grant | | | | | | Authentication method | Bearer authentication | OAuth2 client credentials grant | | Tenant URL | https:// /api/v2/scim/v2 | https:// /api/v2/scim/v2 | | Secret token | the scim … secret | — | | Token endpoint | — | https:// /api/v2/scim/oauth/token | | Client identifier | — | the scimc … client identifier | | Client secret | — | the scimcs … client secret | Select Test connection . Entra ID calls /Users with the credential, and a correct credential answers 200 . The token endpoint accepts grant type=client credentials with the client identifier and secret in the form body ( client secret post ) or in an HTTP Basic header ( client secret basic ). The operator sets the access token lifetime with ELITEA SCIM ACCESS TOKEN TTL (between 5m and 24h ). Maintenance mode does not stop SCIM. A SCIM client has no administration permissions, and the maintenance gate admits only administrators, so the gate does not apply to SCIM. The identity provider continues to create, update and deactivate accounts during a maintenance window. To freeze the directory, pause provisioning in the identity provider. Each OAuth2 client can hold at most 20 live access tokens. A new token removes the oldest one. Failed token requests are limited per client identifier and caller address. After 20 failures in one minute, that address gets 429 until the minute ends, also with the correct secret. Failures from one address never block another address, so an attacker cannot lock out your identity provider. To know the real caller address behind an ingress, set the proxy networks in ELITEA TRUSTED PROXY CIDRS (or trusted proxy cidrs in the Form authentication document). Without them the caller address is unknown. The endpoint then checks every secret first, so a correct secret is never refused, and it limits only failures. Rotate or revoke a SCIM client Rotate makes a new secret. The old secret stops working immediately, and every access token issued with it stops working too. Put the new secret in the identity provider at once. Revoke stops the client from authenticating. The row stays in the list, so the audit trail can still name it. Delete removes the client. Bind SCIM groups to a project role What the admin console does provide is the group to role mapping, beneath the identity provider list: Name the SCIM group exactly as your identity provider sends it, and choose the project and role it grants. A member the group granted the role to loses it when they leave the group. A member who already held that role independently keeps it — the identity provider is authoritative only over what it granted, not over everything it happens to find. A SCIM group with no binding is refused by name; it never creates a project on its own, and it never guesses a role. What SCIM may and may not change SCIM manages ordinary accounts: it creates them, renames them, changes their display name and name parts, and deactivates them. A SCIM DELETE deactivates (suspends) the account instead of deleting it, so the person's work stays attached if they return. Some accounts are off limits to SCIM. Any write to them is refused with 403 ( scimType: mutability ), the reason is included in the response, and the refused attempt is recorded in the Audit Trail : Accounts with an administration role (any role on the admin console's Users page). SCIM cannot rename, suspend or deprovision them, including people who became administrators after SCIM created their account. This stops a SCIM credential from taking over or locking out the people who administer the platform. Platform accounts — addresses in the @centry.user domain, such as system@centry.user and the per project system user @centry.user . SCIM also cannot give any account an address in that domain, and a SCIM group cannot grant a project role to a platform account. When your identity provider tries to deprovision someone who holds an administration role, the request is refused with "SCIM deprovisioning refused: account holds an administration role — remove the role, then let the IdP retry". Until then, the person's sessions and access tokens keep working. On the admin console's Users page, remove the person's administration role. You can also suspend them from that page right away. The next provisioning cycle repeats the request, and this time it succeeds. SCIM stores one address per account, and that address is the SCIM userName . A change to the work email alone is accepted but does not change the account's address. Only a userName change does.

title: Branding
text: Branding is a runtime setting, not a build step: changes reach every user on their next page load, with no rebuild or restart required. The brand pack you edit here is what the platform serves to every client on the deployment — there is no per project or per user brand. Edit the brand pack The form is grouped into identity, color/type/shape, assets, and font faces. Every field can inherit from the platform default instead of being set explicitly, and the form says what it would inherit and from where. Logos and other assets are uploaded directly; self hosted font faces are declared here rather than linked externally. A sample surface renders in both light and dark under a theme built from your current draft, including the derived color swatches and a text on primary contrast check. The check is a warning only — it does not block saving. The merged pack becomes what every user's next page load receives. Import, export, and restore a package Download the current brand as a package. Uploading a package runs a dry run first, so you see what would change before committing it. Kept versions can be restored from the package panel. An unsaved draft is respected by the import and restore controls — neither silently discards edits you have not saved yet. What is inherited by default Every branding field defaults to the platform's own look unless you override it. This means a fresh deployment already looks complete without any editing here — Branding is where you replace that default with your organization's identity, one field at a time, not something you must fully populate before it is usable.

title: Budgets and LLM governance
text: Budgets and LLM Governance are two separate admin pages that both shape how the LLM gateway treats a request. Set spend limits Open Budgets . Each row is a project or a project member with a spend ceiling. Search, then open its budget dialog. Choose a monthly limit, or mark it unlimited. The gateway bills on the calendar month; no other period is enforced. Choose whether the gateway fails open (allows calls through) or fails closed (refuses calls) if it cannot reach its budget counter, or inherit the platform default. Open the members drawer to set a spend ceiling for an individual project member, on top of the project ceiling. A budget stored here is only enforced if the LLM gateway is configured with GATEWAY NATS URL . Without it, every number on this page round trips and saves, but no call is ever refused for exceeding it. The page shows a warning only when the gateway itself reports enforcement is off — never from silence. The spend ceiling on this page is set per project and per member only — there is no per agent or per tool spend cap, and setting one is not planned. To see WHICH agent or tool a project's cost came from, open Settings › Analytics on the project and use the Costs tab's Cost by Agent and Cost by Tool tables ( 875). Author LLM governance rules Open LLM Governance . Each row is a scoped rule the gateway reads and enforces on the /llm path: budgets, rate limits, model and MCP server allowlists, credential rate policy, and CEL based routing rules. Choose the scope it applies to (provider, model, or project) and the rule fields for that scope. A saved definition does not take effect immediately — the gateway polls this table on a refresh interval (30 seconds by default) rather than reloading on every write, so a replica that missed an event still converges. A saved rule can still be unenforceable: it may fail to load, or load and match nothing it could ever apply to. The gateway's own status report (surfaced on the LLM proxy Status tab) names any rule it rejected — a save here is not proof the rule is in force.

title: Features and configuration
text: Features and Configuration are two admin pages that share one mechanism: a list of sections, each either editable here or pointing you to where it actually lives. A section that this deployment cannot serve says so, with a reason, instead of rendering a form that saves into nothing. Features Whether Elitea exposes an MCP server at all, and whether MCP servers show in the main navigation. Block agent publishing platform wide, restrict it to named projects, and set the categories offered. The same three controls, for skills. Turn on the project Analytics tab (Settings › Analytics). The links shown on the in app Help Center page. Enable the assistant, and set which project and agent answer it. Turn voice input and text to speech on, or keep the controls visible but disabled. From the list on the left. Only changed fields are sent; Discard reverts unsaved edits. Configuration Configuration holds the sections Features does not: some editable directly here, some pointing to a dedicated page. Blocked toolkit types (a blocked type cannot be listed or created, and is stripped from every agent before it runs — existing toolkits of that type stay visible so an administrator can review and delete them, but stop working); blocked individual tools within an otherwise allowed toolkit; tools that require the user to authorize each call ("sensitive action" tools, matched per toolkit or with for every toolkit); the company name and message template shown in that authorization dialog. A dismissible banner shown across the app, with its own icon, style, and message. Turns on maintenance mode: every caller without administration access gets a 503 and the splash screen, with its own title, message, and optional HTML. The admin console and authentication routes stay reachable so the window is reversible from inside itself. The outbound mail relay: SMTP host, port, TLS mode, credentials, from/reply to addresses, and the public base URL used in links the platform sends. Environment variables ( SMTP HOST and its siblings) provide a second layer underneath these rows; a row set here wins over the environment field by field. These sections carry credentials or need a row editor shape a flat form cannot express, so each is a page of its own: see Authentication, LLM proxy, and Branding. MCP Servers configures the pre built MCP server catalogue; see the MCP integration guides for what that catalogue offers. Stays unavailable on this page specifically, because a governance corpus is a list of scoped rules rather than one value document. See Budgets and LLM governance. A registry for external provider integrations. This deployment publishes none, so the page reports that rather than showing an empty grid. Configuration's "Advanced", "Observability", "Runtime", and "Admin Panel" sections from the legacy admin UI have no counterpart here — their fields addressed process environment variables and mounted files that no form could ever write, so they were removed rather than kept as permanently unavailable placeholders.

title: LLM proxy
text: The LLM Proxy screen lives under Configuration › LLM Proxy in the admin console. It is the platform wide control over the LLM gateway that sits in front of every model call, organized into six tabs. Whether the gateway is reachable, and whether rate limits and budgets are actually enforceable right now. The platform model catalogue and its per project grants. Deployment wide spend by provider and model. A per request log of every call the gateway served. Publish a provider credential once for the whole platform. The default soft alert threshold for budget warnings. Publish a provider platform wide Normally an AI provider credential belongs to one project. Providers & models lets you publish one from the public project instead, so every project can use it without configuring its own copy. Existing platform providers are listed with a status ok indicator — the gateway only ever dispatches to a provider whose endpoint and key resolve, so a row reporting status ok = false is stored and listed but silently never used. Same provider types as a project credential (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, EPAM DIAL, Anthropic, Ollama, Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI, vLLM). A row imported from an older deployment can still hold its key as plain text rather than sealed in the vault. The panel flags this as sealed: false without ever displaying the value; re saving the credential through this screen seals it. Keyless credentials (workload identity) On GKE, a platform provider of type Vertex AI or EPAM DIAL can hold no key. The gateway then signs in with the Google identity of its own pod (GKE Workload Identity). Vertex AI gets an OAuth access token. Set vertex project and vertex location . Leave vertex credentials empty. EPAM DIAL gets a Google ID token, sent as a bearer token. Set api base . Leave api key empty. The token audience is the api base origin; set token audience to use a different one. To enable the mode: Set llmGateway.serviceAccount.annotations to your GKE binding, for example iam.gke.io/gcp service account: elitea llm gateway@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com . Give that Google service account access to Vertex AI, or to your DIAL deployment. Set llmGateway.workloadIdentity.enabled: true . The chart then sets GATEWAY WORKLOAD IDENTITY ENABLED=true . If llmGateway.networkPolicy.enabled is true, it also opens egress to the GKE metadata server, and only to it. The Status tab reports workload identity enabled . Set auth mode to workload identity on this screen. A switch from a key removes the stored key from the row. Use Test connection after you save. The pod's identity belongs to the platform, so only a platform provider can use it. A project credential with auth mode: workload identity is refused when it is saved. The gateway also refuses every row that is not a shared row of the public project ( WORKLOAD IDENTITY NOT ALLOWED ). If the gateway cannot get a token, the request fails with WORKLOAD IDENTITY TOKEN UNAVAILABLE . It never falls back to another credential. Grant a platform model to specific projects Under Models , each platform model carries a share scope: All projects — every project on the deployment can use it (the default for any model saved before this control existed). No project — stored and listed, but offered nowhere. Selected projects — offered only to the team projects you pick. Personal projects are not offered here individually — granting to one would be a grant to a single person, which this screen does not do. Choose the share scope, and for Selected projects , search and pick which team projects. The model becomes available (or unavailable) to the chosen projects' model pickers. credential resolves = false on a model means it names a provider this platform does not currently publish (or none). That, like status ok = false , means the model is stored and listed but never actually served — this screen is where you see why. Read status, usage, logs, and alerts Reports what the gateway currently holds, not what was last saved — a governance rule can be rejected at load, or load but match nothing, and neither looks different from the authoring side. If the gateway is unreachable, the panel says so rather than showing stale numbers as if they were live. Reads the per request billing ledger, deployment wide, broken down by provider and model. This is a report, not a control — nothing here enforces a budget; that happens on Budgets and governance. Reads every request the gateway served, including ones a billing based Usage report would miss entirely — refused by a budget, rejected by policy, sent to an unresolvable model, or failed upstream. The log has no column for a prompt, completion, or upstream error text; the panel states that rather than showing an expandable row with nothing in it. The gateway keeps each row for 92 days and then deletes it. The period covers the widest Analytics preset (Last 90d). A row identifies the user and the project that made the request, the model, the route, the status and the time. So the log is a 92 day record of each user's LLM activity. Anyone with read access to the database, or to a project's Analytics Users tab, can see that record. The period is fixed in the gateway and no setting changes it. One deployment wide default soft alert percentage for budget warnings. A project with its own alert threshold keeps using that value — changing the default here does not override it. Turning alerting off stops the warning only; the gateway still bills and still refuses a call that exceeds a budget. Retries, timeouts, fallback chains, key weighting, and semantic caching are not configurable from here or anywhere else in the product — the gateway runs its defaults for all of them.

title: Admin console overview
text: The admin console is a separate application at /admin/app , distinct from the main Elitea app. It is where an administrator manages the deployment as a whole: users, projects, authentication, the LLM proxy, budgets, branding, and platform wide configuration. Open the admin console Sign in to Elitea normally, then navigate to /admin/app . The console renders only if your account holds at least one administration mode permission — otherwise you see an access denied screen instead of an empty shell. Every individual page still enforces its own permission on the server on every request; the console's own check only decides whether it is worth rendering the navigation at all. Navigation groups The sidebar has two groups. Delete, promote, suspend, and review activity for any account. The permission matrix, across the central, public, and support scopes. Suspend, create, delete, and manage membership for every project. The global secret vault, merged into every project. Application access requests waiting on a decision. Authentication, LLM Proxy, MCP servers, banner, maintenance, e mail, and more, as a set of schema driven sections. The white label pack — colors, assets, and fonts. The outbound mail relay. Feature toggles: MCP exposure, publishing, analytics, Help Center, Support Assistant, Voice. A read only provider registry; most of it reports "not available" rather than data. Which toolkit types this deployment offers, and to which projects. Budgets, rate limits, allowlists, credential policy, and routing rules the LLM gateway enforces. Per project and per member spend limits. The deployment wide record of what happened. Cron schedules and background job status. There is no LiteLLM section. LiteLLM has been replaced by a standalone gateway service; its former admin screen is gone rather than kept as a dead link. A "Service Descriptors" entry is present even though the legacy admin UI never linked to it — it now answers honestly that this platform has no external provider hub, which is more useful than a page nothing could reach. What each page can and cannot decide window injected permission flags in the console are presentation only: they decide what the sidebar shows, never what a request is allowed to do. Every read and write is re authorized on the server against the actual permission that route requires. A typed URL to a page your account cannot use still reaches it — and still gets refused there.

title: Projects
text: The admin Projects page is the deployment wide project list. Every project — team or personal — appears here, regardless of who owns it. This is the one place an administrator sees and acts on every project at once, rather than one project's own Settings page at a time. Manage an existing project Search the table by name. A suspended project's members lose access until it is unsuspended. Both are available from the project's row menu. Export to CSV downloads the current list. Create or delete a project Both actions run a multi step process rather than a single database write: creating a project provisions its record, quota, dedicated schema, permission set, a system user and token, vault secrets and storage buckets together (vectors need no per project store: they live in the platform's vector store, keyed by project); deleting one reverses the same steps, deletes the project's vectors, and ends in dropping the project's schema. Each step's status is tracked individually, and a failed attempt is compensated rather than left half applied. Deleting a project destroys its data irreversibly. There is no undo. Approving a member's project request A member does not have to ask you directly. From the project switcher, + Request a project opens a small form — a name and a justification — that files a request the same way the App Requests moderation pattern already handles application access (see App requests and toolkit types). It lands on this same App Requests page , under the "Project Request" issue type. On App Requests, set the Issue Type filter to Project Request . Approve runs the same multi step creation process described above — schema, permissions, vault, the lot — with the requester made the new project's admin. Reject requires a reason, exactly like any other app request, and creates nothing. Approving names the new project's id in the queue and in the requester's notification; rejecting delivers your reason. Unlike every other request this queue handles, approving a "Project Request" is not clerical: it is the one decision on this page that creates something rather than only recording an answer.

title: Schedules and tasks
text: Two admin pages cover recurring and running work: Schedules & Tasks for the platform's recurring routines, and Tasks for a live view of background jobs. Manage schedules Open Schedules & Tasks . It lists every recurring routine the platform runs: the scheduled jobs of the main service (index schedule scan, pipeline schedule scan, artifact retention, token expiry notices) and the workers of the scheduler service (price sync and the retention sweeps). Each row shows the schedule in force, whether the routine is on, when it last ran and its outcome, and when it runs next. The switch stops a routine from running without deleting anything. A routine that is switched back on waits for its next scheduled time; it does not replay the runs it missed. Click the schedule and enter an interval such as 30m or 6h , or five cron fields. Each routine has a shortest allowed gap, and a faster schedule is refused with the reason. Leave the field empty to go back to the default that the deployment sets. Changes apply within about a minute, without restarting anything. Every change is recorded in the audit trail with who made it. What a routine does is fixed in code and cannot be edited here: only whether it runs, and when. The editing controls need the configuration.scheduling.schedules.edit permission; with only the view permission the page is read only. If the scheduling registry cannot be read, the main service's scheduled jobs pause until it can, rather than running unchecked. See what is running Open the separate Tasks page for a live view of background work this platform actually tracks: index runs, agent turns, toolkit tool calls, scheduled occurrences, and evaluation runs. Narrow the list to one kind of task. The cancel control only appears on rows the server reports as cancellable — a task past that point does not offer it, rather than offering a control that would mostly answer with a conflict. There is no start control and no log tail here. Starting a task and reading its output are not modeled by this page — a task's output is its own artifact rather than a live log stream.

title: Secrets
text: Admin Secrets is a different store from a project's own Settings › Secrets page. A project's vault serves only that project; the global vault edited here is merged into {{secret.…}} resolution for every project on the deployment. Use the global vault for a value every project should be able to reference — a shared API key for an internal tool, a company wide webhook target — instead of copying the same secret into each project's own vault, where it would need to be kept in sync by hand. Manage a global secret The table lists every global secret by key; values are masked. Give it a key and a value. Reference it from any project as {{secret. }} , the same placeholder syntax used for a project scoped secret. A write here is platform wide — it changes what every project resolves for that key. There is no "hide" control for a global secret. A masked value already hides the secret; a separate hide action exists on neither this page nor its server route. The Internal tab is read only for every administrator, including super admins. It groups entries the platform wrote for itself rather than ones an operator authored — recognized by name ( auth token , project llm key , and bare 32 character hex reference names minted for configuration credential fields), not by a separate server flag. Those rows are shown rather than hidden so the vault's contents are fully accounted for, but nothing here offers to edit a value with no way of knowing what it is for.

title: Users and roles
text: Users and Roles are two related admin pages: Users acts on individual accounts, and Roles defines what each role is allowed to do. Manage users Open Users in the admin console. The table lists every account on the deployment, with search. Search by name or e mail. From the row menu: delete the account, grant or revoke the global admin role, or suspend/unsuspend it. A suspended account cannot sign in. Open the activity drawer for a per user view built on the same audit data as the Audit Trail page. Export to CSV downloads the current list. Invitations do not have a dedicated accept invite page. A new member accepts an invite by signing in; the invite is resolved by matching their identity on first login. Edit roles and permissions Open Roles . It shows a permission matrix across three scopes, each a tab: Central — the administration mode roles used across the deployment (the ones this admin console itself is gated on). Public Project — roles available inside the shared public project. Support Project — roles for the support project, if one is configured for this deployment. If none is configured, this tab reports that rather than an empty grid. Click a cell to grant or revoke that permission for that role, within the selected scope. Use the controls above the matrix. A new standard role only reaches projects that already exist once you use Apply to Projects next to it — creating the role does not retroactively push it everywhere by itself. The super admin column is disabled for anyone who is not a super admin, in the console only — this is a display convenience, not an enforced rule. The server does not treat super admin specially beyond the permission checks that apply to any other role.

title: GitOps with ArgoCD
text: deploy/argocd/ is the GitOps composition for the Kubernetes path: one root Application that renders every child Application under deploy/argocd/applications/ . There is one child, elitea , because there is one chart: the platform, NATS JetStream with its stream bootstrap, and the vector store are all in the elitea chart. There is no umbrella chart; an earlier one ( deploy/helm/elitea platform/ ) was scaffolded and never built, and was removed once app of apps replaced it. Deploy on GKE with Argo CD is the complete walkthrough, with a copyable example in deploy/argocd/examples/gke/ : the published OCI chart, values gke.yaml , secrets from Google Secret Manager through External Secrets, and the GKE Ingress. Apply the root once This is the only object you apply by hand. kubectl apply f deploy/argocd/ (no R ) reaches only this file — the children come from ArgoCD reading the directory, not from a second kubectl apply . The root itself is deliberately not one of the children it manages: an Application that enumerated itself could prune itself. Sync order inside the one Application | Phase | Objects | Why this order | | | | | | PreSync | the ExternalSecrets, when externalSecrets.enabled (wave 30 ); the database preparation, the platform and agent state migrations; the workload session Job (wave 10 ) | The Secrets exist before the Jobs that read them. A failed migration aborts the sync, and the previous pods keep serving. | | wave 10 | the NATS StatefulSet and Services, its CA Issuer , server and route certificates, NetworkPolicy, and the elitea nats bootstrap Job, a Sync hook | The streams, KV buckets and the scheduler's consumer exist before anything that dials them. The Job is a Sync hook, not PostSync : PostSync would wait for workloads that wait for the streams it creates. It is idempotent, and Argo CD deletes it once it succeeds. | | wave 5 | elitea vector and Qdrant | The indexing runtime's store, ready before the worker. | | wave 0 | elitea main, elitea web, the scheduler, the LLM gateway, the OTel collector, the edge objects | The platform. | | wave 1 | the agent worker | After everything it calls. | cert manager is a prerequisite: the NATS CA and every NATS identity are cert manager Certificate s, issued from the chart's own namespaced elitea nats ca Issuer. That Issuer is why NATS lives in the platform's namespace. To use a NATS you run yourself, set nats.enabled: false and point natsClient. at it; the bootstrap Job still runs against it unless natsBootstrap.enabled: false . Installs that ran elitea nats , elitea nats bootstrap and elitea as separate Applications move to the one chart with the steps in "One chart: NATS bundled" in docs/UPGRADING.md . Do not just delete the two NATS manifests: the root prunes them, and their finalizers would delete every NATS resource. The steps detach them first and keep the JetStream volume. Where each value comes from deploy/argocd/applications/elitea.yaml states every value in one spec.source.helm block — nothing reaches the release from anywhere else: valueFiles: [values.yaml] , read from the chart's own repository path. postgresql.existingSecret and postgresql.key — the one database Secret every component derives its DATABASE URL from. NATS needs no parameter: the chart runs it as Service elitea nats in the Application's namespace and issues each client its certificate. llmGateway.env.GATEWAY SELF LLM ORIGINS and llmGateway.egressPosture ship empty in git on purpose — neither can get a safe chart default — and so does the namespace of whatever forwards outside traffic to elitea main ( networkPolicies.main.ingressFrom ). Left empty, the chart refuses to render and the Application reports SyncFailed naming the field, rather than installing a gateway with a disarmed guard. Fill the empty parameters in your own GitOps copy of the file, or imperatively: No secret goes in a parameter. A Helm parameter renders into a ConfigMap, readable by anyone with get on the namespace — the database DSN and every other sensitive value are Kubernetes Secrets that postgresql.existingSecret , runtime.material.secretName and the rest only name . In production, let the chart's externalSecrets block fill those Secrets from your secret manager. Overriding values per environment To point an environment at a different capability set — values standalone.yaml , values gke.yaml , values nats ha.yaml for three NATS nodes, or your own file — add it to spec.source.helm.valueFiles in that environment's copy of elitea.yaml , after values.yaml (Helm merges files in list order, so later files win): Keep one Application manifest per environment (a staging/elitea.yaml , a prod/elitea.yaml , or separate branches/paths per ArgoCD Application 's targetRevision ) rather than templating the Application itself — the file is already the full statement of what an environment installs. Source the published chart applications/elitea.yaml syncs the chart from this repository's main , which suits a development cluster. A production environment should pin a release of the published chart instead: The published chart carries its dependencies (the upstream NATS, Qdrant, KEDA and prometheus adapter charts and the sandbox runtime installer), so an OCI source needs nothing else and is the recommended source. A git source ( path: deploy/helm/elitea ) has no charts/ (it is never committed): Argo CD runs helm dependency build itself from the committed Chart.lock . Every chart repository must be reachable from the repo server and, in an AppProject that restricts sourceRepos , listed there. The list includes KEDA's and prometheus adapter's repositories even while keda.enabled and prometheusAdapter.enabled are false, because helm dependency build fetches every dependency: In an air gapped cluster, mirror the published OCI chart instead: it already carries all four, so nothing else needs mirroring. deploy/argocd/examples/gke/ has the full Application, the repository registration and an example ClusterSecretStore . Image tag promotion Every first party image and every chart is stamped with the same release version by .github/workflows/publish.yml (a stable release you dispatch from main , or a nightly. / dev. pre release, which never moves latest ) — one tag for the whole platform, because a per component tag could only ever express a mistake. Promoting a release is changing the chart version an Application pulls: The published chart's own image.tag already defaults to the chart's version — only override image.tag to pin an environment behind the chart's own release, or to test a release candidate. Read the entries in docs/UPGRADING.md between the two versions first. Rollback ArgoCD's own history covers a sync gone wrong: For a release level rollback (a bad image), point the Application back at a previous chart version and let selfHeal: true reconcile it — the chart's own migration hook still runs on the way there, so a rollback that also needs a schema rollback is a database operation, not something this reconciliation does for you. If a CI release itself failed mid publish, the rollback job in publish.yml already deleted the charts and images it had pushed, so there is nothing half published to roll back to. Your own GitOps repository The deploy/argocd/ and deploy/helm/ in this repository are the template . A production deployment rolls from a GitOps repository your organisation owns, which layers its own values on top of the published chart and gets its secrets from a secret manager — nothing in this repository points at any particular environment. Copy deploy/argocd/examples/gke/ (or the structure of deploy/argocd/ ) into that repository rather than syncing this one. syncPolicy.automated with prune: true and selfHeal: true is set on every Application here, including the root. Removing a file from applications/ is a production deletion of that Application and everything it manages — review those diffs as such. {/ source: deploy/argocd/app of apps.yaml; deploy/argocd/applications/elitea.yaml; deploy/argocd/examples/gke/; deploy/helm/elitea/Chart.yaml (dependencies); deploy/helm/elitea/templates/nats/, templates/natsBootstrap/job.yaml (wave 10, Sync hook); deploy/helm/elitea/templates/externalSecrets/externalsecrets.yaml (PreSync, wave 30); deploy/helm/tests/render nats security.sh (argocd wave checks); docs/UPGRADING.md ("One chart: NATS bundled"); deploy/README.md (composition decision, publish.yml stamping) /}

title: Cloud executor on Kubernetes
text: The cloud executor runs a desktop Local work thread after its owner chooses Send to cloud . Each cloud turn gets its own Pod, the workspace run , in which the agent builds and runs the user's project. That Pod runs untrusted code, so it must never share the node kernel. It runs under a sandboxing RuntimeClass (gVisor or Kata) on dedicated sandbox nodes. The supervisor refuses everything else. This page assumes the platform is already installed (Deploy from scratch). It adds: | Piece | Comes from | | | | | Sandbox nodes and a RuntimeClass whose handler is runsc , gvisor or kata | your platform (GKE, AKS), or the elitea chart's sandbox runtime installer, sandboxRuntime (EKS, k3s) | | The sandbox supervisor and its workspace profile | the elitea chart ( sandboxKubernetes. ) | | The worker's side of workspace runs | the elitea chart ( worker.runtime.workspaceRuns ) | | The egress proxy for projects with a host allowlist | the elitea chart ( egressProxy. ) | | An object store with default encryption at rest | you | | The supervisor's certificate, the run token keys | you (one script below) | By default the elitea chart creates no RuntimeClass and installs nothing on a node. The sandbox runtime is either part of your platform (GKE, AKS) or comes from the chart's privileged installer, sandboxRuntime , which you turn on on purpose. That installer is the elitea sandbox runtime chart carried as a dependency; it is still published on its own ( oci://ghcr.io/elitea ng/charts/elitea sandbox runtime ) for a cluster that installs it separately. Turn it on in one release per cluster : the gvisor RuntimeClass is cluster scoped, and two installers would change the same nodes. Under Argo CD, the AppProject must allow the installer's namespace as a destination. Step 1: sandbox nodes and the runtime Pick your platform. Each tab ends with the three values the elitea chart needs: runtimeClass.name , nodeSelector and tolerations . Create a GKE Sandbox node pool. GKE installs gVisor on it, taints it with sandbox.gke.io/runtime=gvisor:NoSchedule and creates the gvisor RuntimeClass, whose scheduling adds the matching toleration to every Pod that asks for it. No installer is needed. In Terraform, this is node config { sandbox config { sandbox type = "gvisor" } } on the node pool. Add a Pod Sandboxing node pool (Kata VM isolation on Azure Linux). AKS installs Kata and registers the kata vm isolation RuntimeClass. Older clusters name it kata mshv vm isolation . No installer is needed. EKS ships no sandbox runtime. Create a labelled and tainted node group on the Amazon Linux 2023 AMI, then install gVisor with the chart's sandbox runtime installer in containerd mode. Bottlerocket is not supported: its root file system is read only. The installer's DaemonSet runs privileged, so it goes to a namespace of its own that admits privileged pods, not to the platform's namespace. Create it, then turn the installer on in the elitea values and upgrade the release: The installer writes /etc/containerd/config.d/50 elitea runsc.toml . If needed, it adds that directory to imports in /etc/containerd/config.toml . It checks with containerd config dump that nothing else changes, then restarts containerd once. Label and taint the sandbox node, then install gVisor with the chart's sandbox runtime installer in k3s mode, its default. What the installer does on the node: 1. It installs a pinned gVisor release, checked against the chart's SHA 512 and the release's published checksum, as /usr/local/bin/runsc , /usr/local/bin/containerd shim runsc v1 and the sidecars runsc needs in /usr/local/bin/gvisor bin/ . 2. It writes /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config v3.toml.tmpl (or config.toml.tmpl on containerd 1.7): k3s's own base template ( {{ template "base" . }} ) plus a marked runsc runtime block. Content you already have there is kept. 3. It restarts k3s agent , or k3s on a server node, once, and waits for k3s to render the runtime into config.toml . If k3s does not come back, the previous template is restored. To do the same by hand, unpack the release archive ( runsc , containerd shim runsc v1 and the gvisor bin/ directory) into /usr/local/bin and write this template, then run systemctl restart k3s agent : On containerd 1.7 (config version 2), the table is [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runsc] in config.toml.tmpl . Then create the RuntimeClass yourself: handler: runsc , with scheduling.nodeSelector and tolerations for the sandbox node. Check the runtime before going on: Under gVisor, dmesg prints gVisor's own boot lines ("Starting gVisor..."), not the host kernel's. Use your RuntimeClass name and node selector. Before it creates any workspace run Pod, the supervisor reads the RuntimeClass named in sandboxKubernetes.runtimeClass.name and accepts only the handlers runsc , gvisor and kata . It checks at start and again before each run. A missing RuntimeClass, a read the API server refuses, and runc or crun refuse every workspace run, with workspace run runtime class refused in its log (and workspace run runtime class unverified at start). The supervisor itself keeps running, so its other profiles keep working, and a fixed RuntimeClass is picked up within seconds, without a restart. The chart grants it get on that one RuntimeClass, and nothing else cluster wide. Step 2: the bucket Workspace segments are stored in the platform's bucket, or in STORAGE WORKSPACE BUCKET if you set one. Send to cloud stays off until Main confirms at startup that every such bucket has default encryption at rest . RustFS 1.0.0 beta.8 implements default SSE S3 without a KMS, but its master key is a built in all zero key unless you set RUSTFS SSE S3 MASTER KEY (base64 of 32 random bytes) in the RustFS container. Set the key before you add the bucket rule: objects written under one key cannot be read after it changes, so back the key up with your other secrets. The same release also refuses a multipart upload part that carries a checksum into an encrypted bucket. Set main.env.AWS REQUEST CHECKSUM CALCULATION: when required . Main then sends a checksum only where it asks for one (the presigned SHA 256 uploads of workspace segments), so its other uploads go without a per request integrity check. Leave it empty on AWS S3 and on any store that accepts checksummed parts. By default the desktop app uploads and downloads workspace segments with presigned URLs on S3 ENDPOINT URL . That works for AWS S3, or for a store behind an HTTPS ingress. For an in cluster store with no public address, such as http://rustfs:9000 , the desktop refuses the URL with "the store handed out a URL this client does not use". Set main.env.S3 PRESIGN: "false" , and the desktop streams segments through Main instead. The switch covers the whole store, so artifact transfer grants also go through Main. The worker is not affected: it always reaches the store through Main. Three things follow: Each segment goes up in one request, with no multipart upload. Main's ingress must accept a body as large as the largest segment. On ingress nginx, set nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy body size on Main's ingress. Main writes those segments to the store as multipart uploads of its own. On RustFS with default encryption, also set AWS REQUEST CHECKSUM CALCULATION: when required (see the warning above). Bytes move through Main, so size Main's network and CPU for them. The platform's IAM policy needs s3:GetEncryptionConfiguration on the bucket, in addition to the object permissions it already has. A bucket without a default rule is refused. Some S3 compatible stores do not implement GetBucketEncryption . For those only, an operator can attest the encryption with main.env.ELITEA CLOUD EXECUTOR STORAGE ENCRYPTION ATTESTED: "true" . Main logs the attestation at startup and records it in the audit trail. Step 3: keys, certificates and the supervisor material The worker dials the supervisor over mTLS: the worker presents its runtime client certificate, and the supervisor presents a server certificate for elitea sandbox workspace . Both chain to the runtime CA . Main signs a grant for each run, and the supervisor verifies it with Main's public command signing keyring. The egress proxy admits a run with a token Main signs with a separate Ed25519 key. The proxy's audit certificate ( egressProxy.audit ) is a cert manager Certificate that the chart creates on the runtime CA. The chart's default names a ClusterIssuer . Deploy from scratch creates a namespaced Issuer called elitea runtime ca , so the values below set egressProxy.audit.issuerRef.kind: Issuer . Without it the certificate never issues and the proxy never becomes Ready. The supervisor reads the material once, at start. After a rotation, run kubectl rollout restart deploy/elitea sandbox supervisor . The material Secret must not contain a key named workspace.json : that name is reserved for the profile the chart renders. Step 4: the values A k3s cluster with one tainted sandbox node labelled elitea.ai/sandbox=true . For another platform, swap the three values from Step 1. Take the digests from the release you install: crane digest ghcr.io/elitea ng/elitea sandbox supervisor: , and the same for elitea workspace runner . From these values the chart renders the supervisor's workspace profile into a ConfigMap, projects it beside the material Secret, and creates the elitea sandbox workspace Service. It also gives the worker its scratch volume and tells Main that an executor exists ( ELITEA CLOUD EXECUTOR CONFIGURED ). The render fails if workspace runs are only partly enabled: without the supervisor, without worker.runtime.workspaceRuns , without a RuntimeClass, or with an audience or target that does not match. Step 5: turn it on Send to cloud needs four switches, all on. If one is off, the desktop says which one. | Switch | Where | Reason shown when off | | | | | | Cloud executor: Enabled | Admin, Configuration, Cloud executor ( cloud executor.enabled ) | platform off | | The project's own on/off: its explicit value, or else Default for Projects | Default: Admin, Configuration, Cloud executor ( cloud executor.project default enabled ; off on a new install, see the upgrade rule below). Explicit: Admin, Projects, a project's Send to cloud action (any project), or the project's Settings, General, Send to cloud (its project admin). Both store enabled in the project's cloud executor setting; Use the default for projects removes it | project off | | Native client policy: local work allowed and local work cloud handoff | Admin, Configuration, Native client policy , Local work | device off | | A configured executor and confirmed bucket encryption | Steps 2 to 4 | no executor , storage encryption unconfirmed | Enabled always wins: while it is off, Send to cloud is off in every project, whatever the project says. While it is on, a project that turned it on or off keeps its choice, and a project that never chose follows Default for Projects . That includes every project that existed before this switch, so turning Enabled on with the default off (the default) turns Send to cloud on nowhere yet. Turn it on per project, or turn the default on to open it everywhere and let projects opt out. project off covers both an explicit off and a default that is off. Upgrade rule. Until an administrator saves Default for Projects , it equals the saved Enabled . A new install has neither saved, so both are off. A deployment upgraded with Enabled already on keeps Send to cloud on in every project without its own value, as before the switch existed, and the Configuration page shows Default for Projects on. Once you save the field, the saved value wins, whatever Enabled is. Saving other fields of the form does not save it. To close Send to cloud by default after an upgrade, turn Default for Projects off and save. The project setting's other fields (shell, network and its allowlist, history, caps, exclusions and environment rules) can only narrow the platform values. The Cloud executor section also sets the sandbox ceilings: shell, network and its host allowlist, full history, the segment and file caps, idle retention and return grace, and the exclusions and environment rules. Step 6: verify Then send a Local work thread from the desktop app and start a turn. While it runs: The Pod runs on a sandbox node with your RuntimeClass, and dmesg shows gVisor, not the host. A project with a host allowlist reaches only those hosts. egress proxy.run summary in the proxy's log, and the turn's audit event in Main, list the hosts reached and refused. To prove the refusal, point sandboxKubernetes.runtimeClass.name at a RuntimeClass with handler: runc in a test cluster. The supervisor must refuse every workspace run, with workspace run runtime class refused in its log. Troubleshooting | Symptom | Cause | | | | | "turned off for this deployment" ( platform off ) | The Cloud executor section is not enabled | | "turned off for this project" ( project off ) | The project turned it off, or never chose and Default for Projects is off | | "no cloud executor set up" ( no executor ) | sandboxKubernetes.workspaceRuns or the supervisor is off. For a supervisor outside the chart, set main.env.ELITEA CLOUD EXECUTOR CONFIGURED: "true" | | "could not confirm that its storage is encrypted" | No default encryption rule, or the IAM policy lacks s3:GetEncryptionConfiguration . See Main's start up log line cloud executor: default encryption at rest ... is not confirmed | | Every cloud turn is refused, and the supervisor logs workspace run runtime class refused | The RuntimeClass is missing or not isolating, or the chart's ClusterRole was removed | | A run fails with workspace run.unavailable | worker.runtime.workspaceRuns.target does not reach the profile's Service, or the certificate SAN does not match it | | The installer pod is not Ready | Read its init container's log: kubectl n elitea sandbox runtime logs c install . Backups of every config it replaced are in /var/lib/elitea sandbox runtime/backup on the node | | Run Pods stay Pending | No node matches nodeSelector , or the taint is not tolerated. On GKE, the RuntimeClass adds the toleration |

title: Post-install configuration
text: Once the chart has installed and you have signed in as the first administrator (see Install with Helm), most day to day configuration moves into the admin console rather than back into a values file. This page is the map of what still lives where. Identity: OIDC, SAML, SCIM Configure identity providers under Configuration › Authentication in the admin console — see Authentication for the click through. What matters at the deployment level: Sign in is OIDC or SAML. The local username/password (Form) sign in is off by default : main.env.ELITEA FORM LOGIN ENABLED must be "true" for the Form users file to be a sign in path. With it off, the authentication document is still read (the gateway edge and the runtime depend on it), but no Form login page is mounted and no configured password is accepted. Every Form user needs a real address ( email , or attributes.email ); one without is refused at sign in. See docs/UPGRADING.md in the platform repository. The first global admin is a chart/environment setting, not a console one — identity.initial global admins in the auth document, or main.env.ELITEA INITIAL GLOBAL ADMINS . See the Helm install guide. An OIDC only install now gets the configuration plane. Before, only a Form authentication document ( ELITEA AUTH CONFIG FILE ) composed the principal validator the configuration write path needs; now env.OIDC ISSUER URL alone composes it too, as long as ELITEA AI PROJECT ID is set. A deployment with no authentication at all is still refused, in both the chart and the binary. SCIM provisions accounts and groups at /api/v2/scim/v2 . It authenticates with a dedicated SCIM client credential (a bearer secret, or OAuth2 client credentials at /api/v2/scim/oauth/token ), not with a personal access token. Create the client and bind groups to project roles in the console (see Authentication). ELITEA SCIM ACCESS TOKEN TTL sets the access token lifetime (default 1h ). The first global administrator A fresh database seeds only dev@elitea.ai . On a single sign on deployment, this account has no password. Set identity.initial global admins or the equivalent environment variable before you rely on the admin console. E mail: SMTP bootstrap defaults SMTP HOST , SMTP PORT , SMTP USERNAME , SMTP PASSWORD , SMTP TLS , EMAIL FROM , EMAIL REPLY TO and PUBLIC BASE URL are a default layer , not the whole configuration. Admin → E mail writes a second layer into the database, and internal/emailsettings merges the two field by field on every send — the database wins where it has a value. Ship EMAIL FROM and PUBLIC BASE URL at minimum through main.env ; SMTP PASSWORD belongs in the secrets: block (a Secret), never as a plaintext parameter. A change in the console needs no restart or re sync — the merge runs per message. .settings is what the console stored, .effective is the merged document the next message uses, .sources names database / environment / unset per field, and .configured / .reason say whether a message can be sent. ELITEA EMAIL SUPPRESS: "true" renders every message and sends none — the setting for a shadow or staging deployment. It outranks the console. Egress allowlists Two separate allowlists guard two separate outbound paths, both fail closed by default in the dangerous direction: Names the hosts a saved provider credential's api base may point at. It is the floor : the gateway also reads egress allowlist rows from gateway.governance config (edit them at Admin → LLM Proxy → Governance , no re sync needed) and enforces the union . An authored row can only add a destination — nothing an admin authors can withdraw a host the chart named. One grammar for both sources: a bare host, host:port , a .domain wildcard, or a CIDR block. The first entry anywhere turns the restriction on — with none in either source, a credential may name any public host. A private endpoint needs its address named, not only a hostname — bifrost's SSRF safe dialer refuses RFC 1918 and loopback destinations unless an entry explicitly names a private address or block, because the gateway never resolves a name before deciding (that would reopen the DNS rebinding race the allowlist exists to close). Link local addresses ( 169.254.0.0/16 , fe80::/10 — cloud metadata endpoints) are refused no matter what the allowlist says. GET /governance/status on the gateway (proxied at GET /api/v2/admin/gateway/status , and shown on Admin → LLM Proxy → Status ) reports the merged list by source and whether a private destination is actually reachable. Governs where a tenant created webhook may dial. Unset is the safe default : every RFC 1918, ULA and loopback destination is refused, both when a webhook is created and again at dial time (the destination is re resolved, not trusted from create time). Set it only to let webhooks reach a private receiver you control; link local and multicast addresses are refused unconditionally regardless of this variable. This variable is not a named key in values.yaml — set it like any other elitea main environment variable: Governs where elitea main may dial for a Remote MCP server: Load Tools , the OAuth and client registration proxies, and the authorization metadata those servers name. It uses the same grammar and the same split as the webhook allowlist. Unset refuses every loopback, RFC 1918 and ULA destination, and each connection re resolves the host before it dials. Name a private range (for example 10.0.0.0/8 ) to let users reach MCP servers on your internal network. Link local and multicast addresses stay refused whatever this variable says. Budgets need GATEWAY NATS URL Admin → Budgets writes spend ceiling rows, but the LLM gateway is what enforces them, through a NATS JetStream counter — GATEWAY NATS URL names that server. In Kubernetes the chart derives it from the top level nats block as tls://elitea nats. .svc.cluster.local:4222 , in the platform's own namespace, and mounts the gateway's NATS client certificate beside it; an override must also be tls:// and carry no credential. Leave it unset and the gateway starts, logs a warning, and serves /llm with no budget enforcement : every budget write still answers 200, every limit reads back exactly as authored, Settings → Usage still reports accrued spend — and no call is ever refused. GET /governance/status 's rate limits enforceable is false exactly when this is the case, and Admin → Budgets raises its own warning banner from that field once any budget row exists. The Compose standalone stack runs no NATS service and leaves this unset deliberately, for the same reason. Worker implementation: python (default) or rust worker.implementation selects which agent worker image the chart runs; the values are not interchangeable and the chart handles the difference rather than the operator. Every catalogued toolkit type and every internal chat agent tool is available, at the cost of the larger interpreter/dependency image. This is the default in both the Helm chart and standalone stack.sh . A smaller, faster process with the platform's native agent runtime (checkpointing, step limit enforcement) and no Python dependency surface — but, as of this release, 18 toolkit types are unimplemented ( ado boards , ado plans , ado repos , ado wiki , aha , bitbucket , confluence , figma , plain gitlab , jira , PowerPoint, qtest , TestIO, TestRail, XRAY Cloud, Zephyr Enterprise, Zephyr Essential, Zephyr Scale) and six internal chat agent tools are skipped with a visible notice instead of run (Image creation, Data Analysis, Elitea MCP Tools, Planner, Swarm Mode, Smart Tools Selection). Every tile still shows, greyed with a reason, rather than disappearing. runtime.json — the worker's own configuration document — is byte identical either way; only the process and its capability surface differ. Object storage and artifacts main.env.STORAGE BACKEND / STORAGE CONTAINER point at an S3 compatible bucket. It must exist before the first sync — the readiness probe tolerates a missing bucket, but the very next boot step (setting the bucket's retention lifecycle) does not, so a missing bucket looks like a green install that then crash loops. objectInit.enabled: true creates it for a self hosted S3 compatible endpoint you administer directly (RustFS, MinIO); a managed cloud object store almost always withholds CreateBucket from an application scoped credential, so create it out of band there. DeepWiki and Inventory: disk needs Both are the same pattern — a Go subapp host serving the SPI, reaching an engine sidecar over a Unix socket (for DeepWiki the Rust native elitea deepwiki engine native image, for Inventory the Rust native elitea inventory engine image). Both are on by default , and each is one switch : deepwiki.enabled / inventory.enabled . The chart derives elitea main's side from the provider's block — ELITEA DEEPWIKI ENABLED / ELITEA INVENTORY ENABLED , the git allowlist (copied from deepwiki.env / inventory.env ), the client certificate paths and mounts, and the platform gRPC target — so the two halves cannot drift apart. A main.env value that agrees is kept; one that disagrees fails the render with the switch to set instead. To leave either out, set enabled: false explicitly. The one value the chart cannot default is the git allowlist ( ELITEA DEEPWIKI GIT ALLOWLIST , ELITEA INVENTORY GIT ALLOWLIST ): the render lists it with every other missing value in one message. Their callback client certificates ( elitea deepwiki callback client , elitea inventory callback client ) are issued by cert manager from the elitea runtime ca issuer, and their identity Secrets have fixed names ( elitea deepwiki secrets , elitea inventory secrets , key identity secret ). DeepWiki's engine is one Rust binary ( elitea deepwiki engine native ), and its native runner needs a PostgreSQL URL ( deepwiki.secrets or postgresql.existingSecret ); the chart refuses to render without one. Inventory's engine is likewise one Rust binary ( elitea inventory engine ): its native runner needs a PostgreSQL URL ( inventory.secrets or postgresql.existingSecret ) and its own git allowlist, because it clones sources itself; the chart refuses to render without either. Both native runners keep their dense vectors in Qdrant through elitea vector, not in PostgreSQL, so each also needs vector.enabled (on by default, with the bundled Qdrant; or deepwiki.env.ELITEA DEEPWIKI VECTOR URL / inventory.env.ELITEA INVENTORY VECTOR URL naming an elitea vector deployed elsewhere); the chart refuses a native runner with neither. Graphs a previous Python engine left in a toolkit's bucket move over with the import graph tool or the import graph command. The Python DeepWiki and Inventory engines are removed; upgrading from it is in docs/UPGRADING.md . Each provider's scratch space ( deepwiki.scratch 8Gi , inventory.scratch 20Gi by default) is ephemeral clone/index space, not durable storage — a wiki publishes to PostgreSQL, and a replica that dies mid generation only loses work already being redone. ELITEA DEEPWIKI GIT ALLOWLIST / the Inventory equivalent are read fail closed by both halves (the facade and the provider); two values that disagree mean an invocation that starts and then fails. See DeepWiki and Inventory for the product facing side. Observability Traces flow over OpenTelemetry to the chart's own otelCollector (on by default, otel/opentelemetry collector contrib ), which receives OTLP from elitea main, elitea scheduler and elitea main's own tracing ingest proxy. The shipped pipeline exports to debug (log only) — swap the otelCollector.config exporter for a real sink (an OTLP/HTTP endpoint, a vendor backend) before relying on traces outliving the pod. There is no bundled Langfuse or third party APM integration; every other component's OTEL EXPORTER OTLP ENDPOINT should point at the collector's Service ( http:// :4318 in namespace). Enterprise credential governance Off by default. main.env.ELITEA ENTERPRISE CREDENTIAL GOVERNANCE ENABLED pins every new run to a governed profile and an immutable policy revision, mounts the agent identity admin API, and can require an external Vault/OpenBao store. See Enterprise credential governance before you turn it on. Maintenance and the banner Both are console editable under Configuration , not chart settings: a dismissible banner with its own icon/style/message, and a maintenance mode that answers 503 with a splash screen to every caller without administration access (the admin console and authentication routes stay reachable, so the window is reversible from inside itself). See Features and configuration for the click through. {/ source: deploy/README.md:343 388 (SMTP layering), deploy/README.md:766 857 (egress, GATEWAY NATS URL); services/elitea main/internal/api/webhook/ssrf.go:1 90 (webhook allowlist); deploy/helm/elitea/values.yaml:1076, 1120, 1175 (deepwiki/inventory/index types env keys), 2568 2760 (deepwiki/inventory blocks), 2896 2969 (worker.implementation), 3374 3448 (otelCollector); deploy/helm/elitea/templates/main/configmap.yaml:8,64 (main.env is a free form map) /}

title: Credential governance runbook
text: This runbook is the operator procedure for Enterprise credential governance. That page explains what each part does. This page says what to run, in what order, and what to check. The commands assume a Kubernetes install from the elitea chart in namespace , and an administrator's personal API token in $TOKEN . Every admin route below is mounted only while the flag is on. With the flag off, each one answers 404. Prerequisites A release that contains migration 0193. The migration Job applies it on upgrade. An administrator who holds models.agent identity.bindings.manage , and a second administrator who holds models.agent identity.bindings.approve . Activation is a two person step. Both people are read from the caller's token, never from the request body. A role that holds the models.credentials.governed. permissions in each project that will run governed agents. No role holds them by default (see Credential use grants). A policy revision stored with elitea main credential policy put and named in main.env.ELITEA CREDENTIAL GOVERNANCE POLICY REVISION . To keep static secrets in Vault/OpenBao: the ELITEA SECRETSTORE VAULT variables on elitea main, a KV v2 mount with cas required on, and two roles, credential broker (read) and credential migration (create and read). Both roles need the paths elitea/projects/ /credentials/ . The nats CLI, in the natsio/nats box image that the chart's bootstrap Job uses. Check the governed durables Governed commands travel on elitea.rt.v1. .g. . Only three durables read them, one per stream: | Stream | Durable | | | | | ELITEA RT V1 VALIDATE | elitea configuration worker governed v1 | | ELITEA RT V1 AGENT | elitea agent worker governed v1 | | ELITEA RT V1 INDEX | elitea index worker governed v1 | NATS accepts mTLS clients only, and its NetworkPolicy admits port 4222 only from the platform's own pods. So run the CLI in a pod labelled like the bootstrap Job, as the runtime account's bootstrap identity: Inside the pod: Each durable must exist and filter on its .g. subject. "Waiting Pulls" above zero means a governed worker is bound to it, and "Unprocessed Messages" is the governed backlog. A missing durable means the bootstrap Job has not run on this release. Sync the release again, or run helm upgrade again, and wait for elitea nats bootstrap to succeed. Enable Turn the flag on only after governed workers run. Otherwise governed commands wait in their streams and fail at their deadline. Set worker.governedContext: "true" and roll the worker out, with the flag still off. The worker then binds the governed durables next to the legacy ones. Check that "Waiting Pulls" is above zero on all three durables. kubectl n exec deploy/elitea main /elitea main credential policy show id must print the revision you will boot with. Set main.env.ELITEA ENTERPRISE CREDENTIAL GOVERNANCE ENABLED: "true" and main.env.ELITEA CREDENTIAL GOVERNANCE POLICY REVISION: " " . Leave worker.governedContext set: when it is empty, the worker follows the flag. elitea main refuses to boot when a command stream lacks its governed durable, and when the revision is missing or does not match its digest. GET /api/v2/admin/credential references?project id= answers 200 rather than 404. Every new run is pinned governed: Stage credential references A governed run resolves a toolkit credential only by its exact credential reference id , which only the governed admin API writes. Existing toolkits hold configuration references by title. migrate references proposes and stages one credential reference, with its target binding, for each configuration that a governed agent needs. | Flag | Meaning | | | | | dry run | The default. It lists the proposals and writes nothing, because the database session is read only. | | apply | Stage the references. apply writes the state staged only, never active . | | operator | Required with apply . The numeric id of an existing user, recorded as staged by . That user can never activate the reference. The id is compared as a number, so 007 is user 7. An id that is not a number, or names no user, is a usage error (exit 2) and nothing is written. | | project | One tenant project. If you leave it out, every project is read. | | copy to vault | With apply , copy each static secret from the built in vault to Vault/OpenBao (see below). | | policy revision | With copy to vault , the revision that the secret store calls name. It defaults to ELITEA CREDENTIAL GOVERNANCE POLICY REVISION . | | json | One JSON object per toolkit per line, instead of the table | The exit code is 0 when the run finished, 1 when it stopped on an error, and 2 for a usage error. The command is idempotent. Each reference is keyed by its source ( configuration: : , or mcp: ), so a second apply stages nothing new and reports exists . Toolkits that share a configuration share one reference. A retired reference no longer holds its source: the next apply stages a new reference for it and reports staged . What it covers. Each line has an action : propose (in a dry run), staged , exists or skipped with a reason . | Toolkit type | Target | Class | | | | | | jira , confluence | base url | static secret when token or api key holds a {{secret.NAME}} reference. Otherwise oauth delegated . | | qtest | base url | static secret from qtest api token , or oauth delegated | | aha | base url | static secret from api key , or oauth delegated | | sharepoint | site url | oauth delegated | | mcp | the toolkit's url | oauth delegated | A static secret stays where it is, in the built in vault ( backend pgvault , generation 1), unless you pass copy to vault . | Reason | Meaning and what to do | | | | | provider not governed | No governed adapter exists for the type. Its toolkits stay legacy. | | private credential not governed | The toolkit names a private (personal) configuration. Move the credential into the project. | | configuration not in project | The title does not resolve in the toolkit's own project. A governed run never reads the personal or public project. | | secret not sealed | The secret field holds plain text. Save the configuration again so the secret is sealed, then rerun. | | credential reference ambiguous | The toolkit names more than one configuration | | configuration type mismatch , configuration unreadable | The configuration is not the toolkit's type, or its data does not parse | | target not canonical | The target URL is not a plain https origin and path | | class not supported | The adapter does not accept the class | | toolkit not governable | An MCP toolkit with static headers , or without a usable URL | | settings unreadable | The toolkit's stored settings are not a JSON object, so the rule cannot read them. Save the toolkit again, then rerun. | Copy to Vault/OpenBao. copy to vault reads each static secret from the built in vault (it needs SECRETS MASTER KEY ). It stages the reference first, at generation 0, and then writes the secret to /elitea/projects/ /credentials/ with check and set 0, through the secret write ledger. The reference then takes the version that was written as its generation. A reference at generation 0 cannot be activated. Each copy appends a credential reference.copy to vault audit decision, whose id authorises the read, and the decision and the ledger row both name the staged reference. If a run stops between the staging and the write, the next run finishes the copy for the same reference. If the path already holds a secret, the run reads the path's current version. It uses that version when the value is the same, and stops when it differs. Nothing is ever overwritten. Jira Cloud and Confluence Cloud with basic auth: only the token moves. The username is not part of the staged secret. Activate, attach and grant Do these through the admin API. Each write appends a security audit decision in the same transaction. | Route | Permission | Body | | | | | | GET /api/v2/admin/credential references?project id= | bindings.manage or .approve | Query: state , limit , offset | | GET /api/v2/admin/credential references/{id} | bindings.manage or .approve | | | POST /api/v2/admin/credential references/{id}:activate | bindings.approve | {} | | POST /api/v2/admin/credential references/{id}:retire | bindings.manage | {} | | POST /api/v2/admin/credential references/{id}:attach | bindings.manage | {"project id": 42, "toolkit id": 7} | | POST /api/v2/admin/credential references/{id}:detach | bindings.manage | {"project id": 42, "toolkit id": 7} | | PUT /api/v2/admin/agent identities/{id}/toolkits/{toolkit id} | bindings.manage | {"project id": 42} | | DELETE /api/v2/admin/agent identities/{id}/toolkits/{toolkit id} | bindings.manage | {"project id": 42} , or ?project id=42 | The permissions are the models.agent identity. permissions. A second administrator activates the reference. Only a staged reference with a recorded stager can be activated, and the stager's own activation is refused with 403.
