A reference created before migration 0193 has no stager, so it can never be activated: stage a new one. :attach writes credential reference id into the toolkit's stored configuration reference. The reference's provider must be the toolkit's type, and the toolkit must name exactly one project configuration. A toolkit that is attached to another reference must be detached first (409). An MCP toolkit has no configuration reference, so there is nothing to attach. It is governed by its digest and the one usable grant. Attaching re pins the toolkit. It edits the stored settings, so the toolkit's digest changes (the answer carries the new toolkit digest ). Every agent binding that was pinned to the old digest now fails admission with toolkit digest mismatch , until you pin it again in the next step. :detach restores the old settings and the old digest. PUT /api/v2/admin/agent identities/{binding id}/toolkits/{toolkit id} records the toolkit's current digest for the binding. Pin after every attach, detach or toolkit edit. The binding must be in the toolkit's project, and not revoked. Use the per project grant routes in Credential use grants. A grant is two person too. Drain Drain before you turn the flag off, and before an upgrade whose notes say that in flight governed runs fail. Stop starting new governed work first: pause the governed schedules and triggers, or detach their mandates. Then wait until both queries return 0: The second query counts governed runs that wait for a human answer. Their continuation stays governed. Answer or cancel them. "Unprocessed Messages" on the three governed durables must be 0 too. Rollback Turn the flag off. This is the normal rollback. Set main.env.ELITEA ENTERPRISE CREDENTIAL GOVERNANCE ENABLED: "false" , and keep worker.governedContext: "true" until the drain queries return 0. Then remove worker.governedContext . Check afterwards: GET /api/v2/admin/credential references?project id= answers 404, and so do the other governed admin routes. New pins are legacy: the query in Enable shows only elitea.credential profile.legacy.v1 rows for new runs. Legacy runs resolve toolkit credentials by title again. Every reader except the governed resolver ignores credential reference id , so attached toolkits need no change. The data stays: references, grants, pins and the audit chain are kept for the next enable. Roll the release back. The migration runner refuses a database that has a migration its binary does not know ("database version 0193 is not present in the binary manifest"). So you cannot roll back below the release that added 0193 without a database restore. Turn the flag off instead. Incident response Revoke at the narrowest record that covers the incident. Each transition bumps the record's epoch, or for a credential reference, moves it out of active . The next RedeemCredential re reads the epochs and is denied authority revoked . A running run is refused at its next claim, and cancelled at its next lease renewal. Every replica also drops its cached material through elitea.rt.v1.security.invalidation . No body is needed: each call is POST with an empty body or {} . | Compromised | Call | Effect | | | | | | One credential (leaked secret, wrong target) | POST /api/v2/admin/credential references/{id}:retire | The reference leaves active , so every grant and run that uses it is denied. Retired is final. | | One agent's use of one credential | POST /api/v2/projects/{project id}/credential grants/{id}:revoke (or :suspend ) | The grant's epoch increases by 1 | | One agent version | POST /api/v2/admin/agent identities/{id}:revoke (or :suspend ) | The binding's revocation epoch increases by 1. Its mandates stop too. | | One unattended authority | POST /api/v2/admin/mandates/{id}:revoke (or :suspend ) | The mandate's epoch increases by 1. Its schedules and triggers are refused as not usable at their next fire. | | The agent's external identity | POST /api/v2/admin/external agent identities/{id}:suspend | The binding counts as suspended | Then confirm: The revocation took effect: elitea credential revocation denials total and elitea runtime governed authority revoked total{point} increase. elitea credential revocation deny latency seconds shows how long the first denial took. The audit chain is intact and holds the transition: kubectl n exec deploy/elitea main /elitea main security audit verify tenant . For a leaked static secret, rotate it at the provider as well. Retiring stops Elitea from releasing it, but does not change it. Then stage, activate, attach and pin a new reference. Save the new secret in the configuration, then run migrate references apply again, which stages the replacement. With copy to vault the Vault path is the same for each configuration, and its current version still holds the old value, so the run stops. Write the new value to that path in Vault/OpenBao first. The rerun then pins that version.

title: Enterprise credential governance
text: Enterprise credential governance is an operator switch for deployments that must prove which agent used which credential, on whose authority. With it on, every new run is pinned to a governed profile and an immutable policy revision. Later releases enforce that pin at each credential use. The design is ADR 0039 in the architecture records. A governed run gets a credential only from the broker, and only for an operation in the governed catalogue (Jira, Confluence, qTest, Aha, SharePoint and MCP). Each credential must come through an active credential reference attached to the toolkit, under an approved grant. A governed run gets no project secrets header. A toolkit with no attached reference, or a path the broker does not cover yet, fails closed: scheduled indexing, MCP inside nested agents and saved pipelines, and Entra car authorization references. Stage references with migrate references before you turn the flag on. Off by default main.env.ELITEA ENTERPRISE CREDENTIAL GOVERNANCE ENABLED is "false" by default. With it off: Admissions, routes and wire bytes are unchanged. The governed admin routes return 404. No new dependency is built or dialled: no Vault/OpenBao client, no audit relay. The new tables and columns (migrations 0180–0193) are created on upgrade and stay empty. The value must be exactly "true" or "false" . Anything else, such as "1" or "TRUE" , refuses boot rather than picking a profile. Turn it on 1. Write a policy document. It holds parameters only, never a secret: allowed identity modes takes dedicated agent , runtime domain binding and elitea native . A revision that allows none is refused, because then no agent could ever use a governed credential. Unknown fields are refused too. 2. Store it as a revision. Revisions are immutable: a change is a new id. put runs the same checks boot runs (see below), so a revision that could not boot is refused when you publish it. 3. Point the deployment at it and set the flag: Boot refuses to start when the revision is missing, its stored bytes no longer match its digest, it allows no identity mode, the security audit outbox is missing, or it lists a vault required credential classes entry while no Vault/OpenBao store is configured. What a run records Every new run is pinned to elitea.credential profile.governed.v1 and the active revision, in the same transaction that admits it. A pin never changes. A resumed run (a human in the loop answer, a continued agent turn) keeps the pin it started under, even if the flag or the revision changed since. A run with no pin is legacy. The same transaction stores the run's execution security context : the policy revision and digest, the tenant project, the subject and actor chain, the calling application, and the agent version's active identity binding. It holds references, epochs and digests only, never a credential. It is immutable. Every worker command of the run carries the context's digest inside the signed command, so a worker can prove it holds the context Main admitted. A binding is recorded only when exactly one binding of the agent version is active. With none, or more than one, the context names no binding, and every governed credential use of the run is denied. Governed workers A governed run's commands go out on their own NATS subjects, elitea.rt.v1. .g. , and only the governed durables elitea configuration worker governed v1 , elitea agent worker governed v1 and elitea index worker governed v1 read them. The NATS bootstrap Job creates them beside the legacy durables. A worker that does not verify the context never binds them, so a governed command never reaches it. The chart opts the Rust worker in with the same flag: it sets ELITEA WORKER GOVERNED CONTEXT from main.env.ELITEA ENTERPRISE CREDENTIAL GOVERNANCE ENABLED , so Main and the worker cannot disagree. Outside the chart, set it yourself ( true / false ; any other value refuses startup). An opted in worker: binds the governed durables next to the legacy ones; tells Main on each claim that it verifies the context; before it reads any input, fetches the context under its claim and checks it. It must be this run's, at most 16 KiB, match the signed digest, decode with no unknown field, and name the governed profile. A failed check fails the run as an authorization failure, which is never retried. Main also checks every claim: | Refusal | When | | | | | GOVERNED WORKER REQUIRED | A governed command is claimed by a worker that did not declare it verifies the context | | GOVERNED CONTEXT MISSING | A command without a context is claimed for a run pinned governed | Neither is retried. With the flag on, Main refuses to boot when a command stream lacks its governed subject or durable, so re run the NATS bootstrap Job before turning the flag on. Outside the chart, turn the flag on only when at least one governed worker runs. Governed commands wait in their stream for a governed worker, and a run whose deadline passes first fails. Agent identity bindings and mandates With the flag on, two admin API groups are mounted: | Route | Purpose | | | | | /api/v2/admin/agent identities | List and propose bindings of an agent version to an identity | | /api/v2/admin/agent identities/{id}:approve , :suspend , :revoke | Binding lifecycle | | /api/v2/admin/mandates | List and issue mandates (who authorised an unattended run, for which agent and operations, until when) | | /api/v2/admin/mandates/{id}:approve , :suspend , :revoke | Mandate lifecycle | Four permissions gate them, held by super admin and admin only: models.agent identity.bindings.manage (list, propose, suspend, revoke) and models.agent identity.bindings.approve (list, approve) models.agent identity.mandates.manage (list, issue, suspend, revoke) and models.agent identity.mandates.approve (list, approve) Approval is a two person step: the approver can never be the proposer. A mandate cannot outlive the revision's max mandate ttl seconds , and suspending or revoking a binding also stops its mandates. Every change writes a security audit event. External agent identities A binding in dedicated agent mode names an identity the agent holds at an external provider, such as an Entra agent identity. Those identities have their own admin routes: | Route | Purpose | | | | | /api/v2/admin/external agent identities | List and create external identities | | /api/v2/admin/external agent identities/{id}:provision , :activate , :suspend , :resume , :retire | Identity lifecycle | models.agent identity.external.manage gates every route; it is held by super admin and admin . Activation also needs models.agent identity.bindings.approve , and needs an approved binding: provisioning never activates an identity. All versions of an agent share one identity. A fork gets a new one. While its external identity is not active, a binding is treated as suspended. Retiring takes two steps: the identity is retiring until the provider confirms, then retired . Drift reconciliation An administrator can change an external identity at the provider without Elitea. No provider sends a notice when that happens. So, with the flag on, a reconcile loop compares each record with the provider's live object, for each configured provider. One replica runs each pass; the others wait for the next interval. | Live state at the provider | What Elitea does | | | | | Disabled while the record is active | Record goes to suspended , epoch +1, audit external identity.drift.disabled | | Not found while the record is active | Record goes to suspended , epoch +1, audit external identity.drift.missing | | Recreated, or the immutable id or generation changed | Record goes to replaced (terminal), epoch +1, audit external identity.drift.replaced | | A credential or the owner changed (when the provider reports it) | Record goes to suspended , epoch +1, audit external identity.drift.changed | | An Elitea tagged object with no record | Audit external identity.orphan only; nothing changes | A suspension stops new sessions and every Credential call of the agent at once: each check reads the record's state and epoch. A replaced record can never be resumed. To recover, retire what is left and create a new external identity for the agent. Elitea never re provisions or deletes a provider object itself. Two optional revision fields set the loop. Leave them out to keep the defaults: reconcile interval seconds takes 60 to 86400. reconcile outage threshold takes 1 to 100. A provider outage changes no record. Each pass that the provider fails increases agentidentity reconcile errors total{provider} . A pass cut short by a shutdown, or one that fails on the database, does not count as an outage. After reconcile outage threshold failed passes in a row, new agent sessions for that provider are denied ( provider unreconciled ) on every replica, until a pass succeeds. GET /api/v2/admin/external agent identities/drift lists the open findings, newest first, with each provider's reconcile health ( admission denied , consecutive failures , last success at ). It takes provider , limit and offset , and needs models.agent identity.external.manage . A later pass closes a finding it no longer sees: the record was resumed or retired, the orphan is gone or has a record, or a replaced agent has a new live identity. Elitea native agent assertions Many clouds and identity providers have no agent object, but accept a federated JWT from an issuer they trust: AWS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity , GCP Workload Identity Federation, Keycloak federated client authentication, Vault JWT auth and MCP servers. With the elitea native identity mode, Elitea is that issuer. At each credential use of a governed run, Main signs one short lived assertion for exactly one relying party. No cloud secret is stored. It is active only when all three hold: the flag is on, the active revision lists elitea native in allowed identity modes , and main.env.ELITEA AGENT ASSERTION CONFIG names at least one relying party. Otherwise no key is loaded and the routes below return 404. The external identity uses provider elitea ; provisioning makes no external call. Configuration ELITEA AGENT ASSERTION CONFIG is one JSON document. Unknown fields refuse boot. | Field | Value | | | | | origin | The stable https origin of the issuer. Defaults to DEPLOYMENT URL . Relying parties pin it, so do not change it. | | tenant | The elitea tenant claim. Defaults to the origin's host. | | rotation overlap | How long a new key is published before it signs. Default 24h . It must be more than 5m , the JWKS cache lifetime, so every relying party has fetched the new key before it signs; at most 720h . | | relying parties[].id | A name for logs and adapters | | relying parties[].audience | The exact aud . Each audience names one relying party. | | relying parties[].algorithm | ES256 (default) or RS256 . EdDSA is not offered: AWS and GCP federation do not accept it. | | relying parties[].max ttl | Default 10m , from 30s to 15m | | relying parties[].claims profile | aws , gcp wif , keycloak , vault jwt or mcp | A credential request for an audience that is not configured is denied before anything is signed. Key ring The keys are dedicated to agent assertions and sign nothing else. Boot refuses a key whose id or key material is also the command signing key (which also signs code sandbox owner grants), the code owner TLS key or the egress token key. Each key is a PKCS 8 PEM private key: P 256 for ES256 , RSA of at least 2048 bits for RS256 . Its source is one of: file : an absolute path to a key in a mounted Secret. In the chart, set main.agentAssertion.keysSecret to a Secret that holds only these keys: it is mounted whole at main.agentAssertion.mountPath (default /etc/elitea/agent assertion , mode 0444 ), so each data key es256.pem is read as /etc/elitea/agent assertion/es256.pem . Main follows the Secret volume's links but refuses a link that leaves the mount, and a file or directory writable by group or other. vault : a Vault/OpenBao KV v2 secret, read once at boot through the secret store above, with an explicit version . The read uses workload scope agent assertion , so the role is agent assertion , and needs ELITEA SECRETSTORE VAULT configured. The private key is kept only in the signer and never leaves it. Only the agent session broker reaches the signer; no route signs on request. Rotation To rotate, add the new key with a not before time (RFC 3339) and restart. From not before the key is in the JWKS. From not before + rotation overlap it signs every new assertion. The old key stays in the JWKS until the longest max ttl plus one minute has passed after that, so every assertion it signed can still be verified. Then remove it from the configuration. At most one key per algorithm may leave out not before . JWKS and issuer metadata | Route | Content | | | | | GET /.well known/elitea agent jwks.json | The public keys ( kid , alg , use: sig ) | | GET /agent issuer/.well known/openid configuration | issuer and jwks uri | Both are public and cacheable for five minutes, and carry no tenant data. The issuer is /agent issuer , so a relying party that discovers keys through OIDC metadata (AWS IAM, GCP WIF, Vault oidc discovery url ) finds them under the issuer. Others can use the JWKS URL directly. Claims The JWS header has typ: elitea agent+jwt and the signing key's kid . | Claim | Value | | | | | iss | /agent issuer | | sub | agent: | | aud | The one relying party's audience | | iat , nbf , exp , jti | exp is at most the relying party's max ttl and never past the session's expiry. jti is unique. | | sub profile | ai agent | | agent instance id | : | | elitea tenant , elitea project , elitea binding | The tenant, the project id and the binding id | | elitea version digest | The binding's agent definition digest (SHA 256, hex) | | elitea policy revision | The run's pinned policy revision | | elitea epoch | The external identity's revocation epoch | | elitea user | {"sub": " ", "evidence": "asserted"} , only when the run has user attribution | No email, display name or token appears in an assertion. elitea user is always asserted : Elitea states the user on the basis of a mandate, but the assertion does not prove the user. A relying party must not treat it as a verified user. A policy that needs verified user evidence ( delegated verified ) cannot be satisfied by this provider, An asserted user reaches it only when the policy accepts asserted evidence, which no revision does yet. Suspending or retiring the external identity, or any epoch change, stops signing at once: each assertion re reads the record's state and epoch first. Assertions already issued expire within max ttl . Credential use grants A grant lets one agent binding use one credential, through one toolkit, against one target. Grants live per project: | Route | Permission | | | | | GET /api/v2/projects/{project id}/credential grants | models.credentials.governed.manage or .approve | | POST /api/v2/projects/{project id}/credential grants (propose) | models.credentials.governed.manage | | POST …/credential grants/{id}:approve | models.credentials.governed.approve | | POST …/credential grants/{id}:suspend , :revoke | models.credentials.governed.manage | The five models.credentials.governed. permissions ( use , reveal , manage , probe , approve ) are granted to no role by default. Grant them to a role in Settings → Roles . Approval is two person, as for bindings, and the database enforces it. A use grant never permits reveal, manage or probe, and a grant for one target never permits another. Each credential use is decided by eight gates that must all permit: authentication source, RBAC, entity access, binding, toolkit, grant, operation and delegation or mandate. Any gate's error is a deny. The credential broker calls the decision at each redemption (see below). Governed credential resolution In a governed run, a toolkit's credential is chosen by its exact credential reference id, never by its configuration title. Resolution never leaves the run's project: there is no lookup in the user's personal project or in the public project. A stored configuration reference names its governed credential in an optional field: The toolkit create and update routes refuse this field. Only the governed admin API writes it. Every other reader ignores it, so a legacy run resolves the reference by its title exactly as before. At admission. For a run of an agent version with a usable binding, Main checks every top level toolkit in the frozen version. For each toolkit whose stored settings hold a configuration reference, it checks these rules in order, and the first one that fails refuses the run: | Rule | Code | | | | | The toolkit names one reference, not more. | credential reference ambiguous | | The reference is not private . An isolated personal credential is not governed (customer gate D1). | private credential not governed | | The reference names a credential reference id . A reference with only a title is refused. | credential reference required | | The id is a UUID. | credential reference invalid | | The reference exists in the run's project. | credential reference not found | | The reference is active . | credential reference not active | | The binding has an agent toolkit binding for the toolkit. | toolkit not bound | | The toolkit binding's digest is the stored toolkit's digest. | toolkit digest mismatch | | An active, unexpired grant for the binding, toolkit, reference and target allows use . | credential grant missing | A refused start answers 403 with {"error": "governed credential refused", "code": " "} . If no provider is configured, the consent routes are not mounted and a provider OAuth use is denied with BACKEND UNAVAILABLE . The consent flow 1. The client calls POST /api/v2/credential consent/{provider}:start with project id , agent binding id and target binding id . The caller needs models.credentials.governed.use in the project. The target binding must be for that provider in the project, and the agent binding must be active there. 2. The platform stores a random state value as a digest, bound to the user, the project, the agent binding, the target binding and the provider. It also stores an encrypted PKCE verifier. The state is valid for 10 minutes and can be used one time. The answer is the provider authorization URL, with an S256 PKCE challenge and the exact redirect URI. 3. Open that URL in the user's browser. After the user consents, the provider sends the browser to GET /api/v2/credential consent/{provider}:callback . 4. The callback uses up the state. An unknown, expired, used or foreign state, or one for another user, is refused (400). The platform then checks again that the user holds models.credentials.governed.use in the state's project, that the target binding still exists (404 if not) and that the agent binding is still active (409 if not). It exchanges the code with the PKCE verifier and the same redirect URI, stores the encrypted tokens and writes a security audit event. If the user declines, the answer is 403. If another consent for the same grant finished first, the answer is 409: start consent again. Every refused callback writes a denied audit event. A consent again for an existing grant replaces its tokens. If the provider's answer has no refresh token, the grant keeps the one it already holds. A second consent for the same key replaces the stored tokens. No answer, log or error contains a token, a code or a verifier. How a governed run uses the grant For an oauth delegated Jira, Confluence or Aha! credential, the credential broker reads the grant of the run's own user for the run's project, agent binding and target binding. A run with no user, for example under an autonomous mandate, has no such grant and is denied. With no grant, the use is denied with the reason provider consent required : send the user through the consent flow. The envelope is OAUTH ACCESS with the key access token . Single flight refresh An access token is refreshed when it is less than 2 minutes from its expiry. Atlassian refresh tokens rotate: each one works one time. If two replicas refresh at the same time, one of them gets invalid grant and the grant is lost. To prevent this, a refresh runs one time across all elitea main replicas: In each replica, concurrent callers for one grant share one refresh. Across replicas, the refresh needs a lease row in elitea runtime.credential refresh leases . The lease has a fence number. The new access token and the rotated refresh token are written in one transaction, and only while the fence is still current. A holder whose lease expired cannot write. The other replicas wait. They read the grant again with a bounded backoff with jitter until the new token is there. If the provider refuses the refresh token, the grant becomes invalid , its tokens are deleted and an audit event is written. The user must consent again. On a governed agent run the worker gets every MCP token from the credential broker, which records a decision for each use. Credential broker A governed run gets toolkit credentials only from RedeemCredential , a gRPC call on the runtime content service under the worker's mTLS claim. With the flag off, the call answers UNIMPLEMENTED and runs no statement. Each call names one bound tool invocation: an invocation id, the tool call, the toolkit, the operation, the resource, a digest of the arguments and the credential reference. Main then, in this order: 1. Binds the call to the worker's live claim: the workload, claim id, fence and session, on a RUNNING agent job. A node recovery inspection claim is refused. A failure is a gRPC error, and no secret is read. 2. Checks that the run is pinned governed and that the request's context digest equals the stored context. 3. Checks the credential reference against the one admission froze for the toolkit, and fills it in if the worker sent none (see Governed credential resolution). For a toolkit frozen at its digest alone, it uses the single active, unexpired grant of the run's agent binding for that toolkit that allows use of the operation. If no grant matches, or more than one does, the use is denied. 4. Decides the use through the eight gates. 5. Records the invocation and writes the decision to the security audit chain in one transaction (migration 0188). The same id sent again with the same fields is decided again; with any field changed it is refused. If the audit write fails, the use is denied. 6. Opens the run's agent session at its first redemption, from the stored context, and reuses it after that. 7. Gets the material: Static secret: read from the secret store at the reference's generation. oauth delegated credential, Entra (SharePoint): exchanged on behalf of the user, through the run's delegation or the one its delegated background mandate carries. The exchange asks for the adapter's least privilege scopes (SharePoint: https://graph.microsoft.com/Sites.Selected ). If the adapter names none, it asks for the target's /.default . oauth delegated credential, provider OAuth (Jira, Confluence, Aha!): the access token of the user's provider grant, refreshed one time across replicas when it is near expiry (see Provider OAuth consent). Only the keys that the operation catalogue names for the provider are returned. The first key is required and the others are optional, so a Jira or Confluence PAT stored as a bare token works without a username. A stored JSON object without the required key is denied; it is never sent whole. The redemption is recorded and audited. No material is stored or logged. The answer is an envelope ( STATIC , OAUTH ACCESS or DYNAMIC LEASE ) that expires after 5 minutes or earlier, or a denial: | Code | When | | | | | NOT GOVERNED | The run is not pinned governed | | CONTEXT MISMATCH | The digest is not the stored context's, or the context does not match the pin | | INVOCATION MISMATCH | The invocation id was used before with other fields | | DENIED | A gate refused, the audit write failed, the session could not open, or the material has the wrong shape. The denial carries the decision id. | | AUTHORIZATION REQUIRED | Entra asks the user to consent again. The denial carries an opaque authorization reference. A run that is not a chat turn gets DENIED instead. | | CLASS NOT SUPPORTED | The credential class has no adapter or the catalogue names no keys for it | | BACKEND UNAVAILABLE | The secret store, the token endpoint or the delegated token store is not available | The broker reads Vault/OpenBao as the workload scope credential broker , so create the role credential broker when a revision requires Vault. The client token of a governed run GetEliteaClientToken still serves a governed run its token, because the worker uses it for model calls and embeddings. The response carries no project secrets header value. Governed toolkit credentials come only from RedeemCredential ; the client token is limited to the model path. There is no refusal of the client token for governed runs. The token is the same token that a legacy run gets: no issuer that limits a token to the model gateway exists yet. Which authority a run uses Admission records exactly one authority source in the run's security context. Admission picks it from these rules, checked in order: 1. A run started by a signed in user, with a delegation. The run uses that user's newest active, unexpired Entra delegation for the bound agent. A delegation belongs to the user through the sign in that created it. 2. A run started by a user, with no delegation. The run uses the one active delegated background mandate of the binding that names that user. 3. A run with no user. The run uses the one active autonomous mandate of the binding. If no rule matches, the run records no authority. If two mandates match, it also records none. In either case, every credential use of the run is denied. An autonomous mandate never serves a run that has a user. The choice is fixed at admission: a delegation or mandate created later does not change a run that is already running. Whose permissions an autonomous run uses A run under an autonomous mandate has no signed in user. Its RBAC and entity access are those of the user who approved the mandate, read at each decision, so a revoked role takes effect at the next use. The audit chain records that subject as attributed , not verified. A mandate with no approver has no subject, and every use is denied. A delegated background mandate keeps the run's own subject, as an interactive run does. Metrics elitea credential redeem total{result,kind,reason} counts redemptions ( result is permit , deny or error ), and elitea credential redeem duration seconds{result} times them. They carry no tenant or user label. Revocation and caching Every governed authority record has an epoch that each change bumps by one: the agent identity binding, the mandate, the delegation, the credential use grant, the credential reference (its generation) and the external agent identity. PostgreSQL is the authority for all of them. Main checks the epochs a run depends on at three points, for governed runs only: | Point | What is checked | When an epoch is stale | | | | | | ClaimCommand | The binding, mandate and delegation the run's security context recorded at admission | The claim is refused with AUTHORIZATION FAILED ("The governed execution's authority was revoked."), not retryable, and the run is cancelled | | RenewLease | The same, after the fence renewed | The answer is desired state CANCELLED (reason AUTHORITY REVOKED in the log and metric), and the run is cancelled durably | | RedeemCredential | The same, plus the decision's grant and credential reference and the binding's external identity | DENIED (reason authority revoked ), before any cache lookup or secret read | A record that is missing, revoked, suspended, expired or not active counts as stale at any epoch. All the epochs of one check are read in one statement. A legacy run is never checked: its claim is unchanged, and its lease renewal reads only whether the run has a security context (once per replica). With the flag off, none of these checks exists. Cache. Each Main replica keeps a bounded in memory cache of released material, keyed by the full security key: tenant project, agent binding, subject, authority, credential reference, target, scopes and operation class, policy revision and credential generation. An entry stores the epochs read when it was filled. It is served only if the epochs read for this redemption are the same and the entry is not within the skew of its expiry; anything else evicts the entry and zeroes its value. Entra on behalf of access tokens are cached until their expiry. Static secrets are not cached unless the run's policy revision allows it. The cache parameters are optional revision fields; the defaults are test values, not a commitment: The replica's bounds come from the revision Main booted with. Whether a run may reuse a static secret comes from the revision the run is pinned to. A document without cache keeps its digest. Invalidation. After a binding, mandate, delegation, grant or external identity change commits, Main publishes the record's kind, id, new epoch and change time on the core NATS subject elitea.rt.v1.security.invalidation , and every replica drops the entries filled at an older epoch. The message carries no tenant secret and no value. The chart grants the subject to the elitea main runtime identity only; workers are denied it. Delivery is advisory: a lost message costs latency only, because every redemption re reads the epochs. Outages. If PostgreSQL cannot answer the epoch read, new redemptions are denied BACKEND UNAVAILABLE , even when a cached entry exists. If Entra's token endpoint is unavailable, oauth delegated redemptions that miss the cache are denied the same way. Each dependency has a circuit breaker: after 5 consecutive failures it opens for 10 seconds and denies without trying. The Entra breaker is kept per tenant, so one tenant's failing identity provider does not deny another's. A request that the caller cancelled or that ran out of time does not count as a failure. No entry is ever served past its expiry. Metrics. None carries a tenant or user label. | Metric | Meaning | | | | | elitea credential cache lookups total{result} | Cache lookups: hit , miss , stale (epochs changed) or expired | | elitea credential invalidation received total{source} | Invalidations this replica received, local or remote | | elitea credential revocation denials total{change time} | First redemption denied after an epoch change; known when this replica heard of the change | | elitea credential revocation deny latency seconds | From the epoch change to that first denial | | elitea runtime governed authority revoked total{point} | Governed runs refused at claim or cancelled at renew | Mandate bound schedules and triggers With the flag on, a pipeline schedule, an inbound pipeline trigger and an index schedule run only under a mandate that an administrator attached to them. The schedule's author, the trigger's creator and the project system token are no longer an authority for the run, and nothing falls back to them. With the flag off, all three behave as before: saving a schedule still makes the caller its author. Attach or detach a mandate with these routes. They are gated on models.agent identity.mandates.manage and mounted only with the flag on: | Route | Target | | | | | PUT , DELETE /api/v2/admin/mandate attachments/pipeline schedules/{project id}/{version id} | The pipeline version's schedule | | PUT , DELETE /api/v2/admin/mandate attachments/pipeline triggers/{project id}/{version id} | The pipeline version's live inbound trigger | | PUT , DELETE /api/v2/admin/mandate attachments/index schedules/{project id}/{toolkit id}/{index name} | The schedule of one index | PUT takes {"mandate id": " "} . The attach is refused with 409 and a code unless all of these hold: the mandate is in the target's project ( MANDATE TENANT MISMATCH ); its kind is autonomous or delegated background and the active revision allows it ( MANDATE KIND NOT ALLOWED ). An interactive delegation is never accepted; its binding is bound to the version the target starts ( MANDATE BINDING MISMATCH ); it is not revoked or expired ( MANDATE NOT USABLE ). A proposed or suspended mandate can be attached, but it runs nothing until it is active; its resource scopes cover the target ( MANDATE SCOPE MISMATCH ). A revision allows unattended kinds with an optional field. A revision without the field allows none, so every governed schedule and trigger is refused until you list the kinds: Asserted users. A user attended governed run needs authority over its user. A verified delegation (an Entra sign in) gives it. Otherwise it comes from an approved delegated background mandate that names the user, and then the agent session carries a user Elitea asserts on the basis of that mandate, not one a provider verified. A revision accepts asserted users only for the identity modes it lists, and only elitea native can take one. Without the field, no session carries an asserted user, so every user attended governed run without a delegation is denied with agent session.asserted user not accepted : Each listed mode must also be in allowed identity modes , or the revision is refused. Scopes. A mandate can restrict a schedule with two resource scope prefixes. schedule.cron: names a cron expression with its fields joined by , for example schedule.cron:0 3 . schedule.input:sha256: names the SHA 256 of the schedule's input. If a mandate has neither prefix, it covers any cron and input. A scoped mandate covers nothing that lacks the scoped value: a mandate with a schedule.cron: scope never covers an inbound trigger, and one with a schedule.input:sha256: scope never covers a trigger or an index schedule. An index schedule's mandate must cover the cron of every schedule the index has. Saving a governed schedule keeps its mandate. A save whose new cron or input the mandate does not cover answers 409 MANDATE SCOPE MISMATCH , and nothing changes. At every fire the mandate is checked again. It must be active and unexpired, the epochs of the mandate, its binding and its delegation must be current, and its scopes must still cover the target. The admission then records that mandate in the run's security context, so the lease renewal check cancels the run when the mandate is revoked or expires (see Revocation and caching). A delegated background mandate runs as its subject, whose run permission is still checked at each fire. An autonomous mandate has no subject. For a trigger, the webhook's credential still has to be valid, but it is recorded as the caller and is not the authority. A refused fire starts nothing, writes no admission and appends a security audit decision ( unattended run.admit , effect deny ): | Entry point | No mandate | Mandate not usable | Out of scope | | | | | | | Pipeline schedule | last result skipped mandate required | skipped mandate not usable | skipped mandate scope | | Inbound trigger | 403 , code MANDATE REQUIRED | 403 , MANDATE NOT USABLE | n/a | | Index schedule | Initialization failure whose reason starts with MANDATE REQUIRED | MANDATE NOT USABLE | MANDATE SCOPE MISMATCH | last run is not stamped on a skip. Each attach and detach also appends a security audit decision. A governed index schedule never gets the project system token: neither the occurrence preflight nor the worker's client token request issues it. The broker does not yet release the index.ingest capability, so a governed index run that needs the platform's client token fails closed for now. Vault / OpenBao secret store Governed credentials live in the built in encrypted PostgreSQL vault unless the revision lists their class under vault required credential classes . Those classes need an external HashiCorp Vault or OpenBao KV v2 store, configured only by these variables (read only with the flag on): | Variable | Value | | | | | ELITEA SECRETSTORE VAULT ADDR | https://host[:port] . Plain http is refused. | | ELITEA SECRETSTORE VAULT CA FILE | CA bundle that signs the server certificate | | ELITEA SECRETSTORE VAULT AUTH METHOD | jwt or kubernetes | | ELITEA SECRETSTORE VAULT AUTH MOUNT | The auth method's mount path | | ELITEA SECRETSTORE VAULT ROLE PREFIX | Roles are , one per scope | | ELITEA SECRETSTORE VAULT KV MOUNT | The KV v2 mount. It must have cas required on. | | ELITEA SECRETSTORE VAULT TOKEN FILE | The projected workload token, re read at every login | | ELITEA SECRETSTORE VAULT NAMESPACE | Vault Enterprise namespace. Leave empty for OpenBao and Vault CE. | | ELITEA SECRETSTORE VAULT READINESS SCOPE | The workload scope the boot check logs in as | All empty means "not configured". Setting any one of them makes all of them required: a half configuration refuses boot. There are no defaults for anything that selects authority. Security audit chain Governed events (revisions, bindings, mandates, and later every credential decision) are written to a per tenant hash chain in the same transaction as the change, then relayed to durable storage. A relay or exporter failure leaves rows pending; none is dropped. A backlog above the revision's audit backlog alert threshold raises an alert. Check a chain at any time: The scheduler can delete relayed outbox rows older than a window. SECURITY AUDIT OUTBOX RETENTION DAYS is "0" by default, which deletes nothing. SECURITY AUDIT OUTBOX RETENTION INTERVAL (default 1h ), ... BATCH SIZE and ... MAX BATCHES bound each sweep. Scale (synthetic) These numbers come from one synthetic run. They hold for the dimensions and the machine below, and for nothing beyond them. They are not a throughput claim for a production deployment. Dimensions. 300 teams (projects) × 60 calling applications, 1 agent per application, 2 grants per agent: 18,000 agents, bindings, external identities, delegations and mandates, and 36,000 credential references, target bindings, toolkit bindings and grants, under one policy revision. The seed writes bindings, identities, delegations, mandates and grants through the production stores, so the seed adds 126,000 audit rows. Machine. Apple M4 Pro (14 cores, 48 GB). The test process ran on the host. PostgreSQL 18.6 ran in a podman VM (7 vCPUs, 2 GiB) with stock settings ( synchronous commit=on , 100 connections). NATS 2.12 ran in the same VM. Go 1.26.9. What is real and what is not. The broker, the AND composed decider, the admission transaction, the epoch reads, the refresh coordinator and its lease, the provider OAuth token source and the audit relay are the production code, against a real PostgreSQL. These parts are stubs: the RBAC and entity access gates (always allow), the secret backend (in memory), the identity provider (the fake provider), and the Jira token endpoint (an in process rotating fake that waits 40 ms per refresh). There is no network hop between the replicas and PostgreSQL other than the VM's. Each of the 3 "replicas" is its own pool of 16 connections and its own broker in one process. | Measurement | Load | p50 | p95 | p99 | max | | | | | | | | | Admission, legacy ( 999 method) | 5 bursts of 100 starts, 40 concurrent, 3 replicas | 29.5 ms | 37.4 ms | 41.2 ms | 47.2 ms | | Admission, governed (resolve + freeze + pin + mandate bind + security context) | same | 41.6 ms | 61.1 ms | 66.0 ms | 67.6 ms | | Redeem, spread across 276 teams | 6,000 redemptions, 32 workers, 3 replicas, 1,500 runs (972/s) | 30.9 ms | 43.6 ms | 47.0 ms | 70.2 ms | | Redeem, first of a run (opens the agent session) | 1,500 of the above | 41.1 ms | 46.6 ms | 60.3 ms | 70.2 ms | | Redeem, repeat | 4,500 of the above | 29.9 ms | 34.0 ms | 36.0 ms | 43.6 ms | | Redeem, one team | 3,000 redemptions, 32 workers, 60 runs of one team (407/s) | 63.8 ms | 191.6 ms | 277.5 ms | 381.8 ms | | Refresh contention | 5 rounds × 60 concurrent redemptions of one expiring grant, 3 replicas | 124.1 ms | 189.5 ms | 207.4 ms | 209.5 ms | | Revocation to deny, all kinds | 50 trials (10 each: grant, mandate, binding, delegation, credential reference) | 4.2 ms | 5.2 ms | 5.8 ms | 5.8 ms | | Audit outbox lag (append to durable store) | the redeem loads above, relay at its defaults (1 s, batch 500) | 471 ms | 879 ms | 951 ms | 986 ms | | NATS invalidation fan out | 500 epoch changes, 2 hubs over core NATS | 0.21 ms | 0.30 ms | 0.37 ms | 0.51 ms | What the run also checked: Refresh. Every round made exactly one provider refresh call (5 in total) and no invalid grant , across 3 replicas with their own coordinators. All 300 contended redemptions were permitted. Revocation. No redemption that started after the revocation committed was permitted, on a replica other than the writer. The broker re reads the epochs on every redemption, so the deny does not depend on the invalidation fan out. Revocation to deny is about one redemption's duration. Audit. The relay drained the seed's 126,000 rows at about 29,000 rows/s before the load. During the load the backlog peaked at 2,158 rows. The lag is set by the relay interval. Every outbox row reached the durable store with its hash. One team. A team's audit events form one hash chain. Every append takes that chain's head row until its transaction commits, so a single team's redemptions serialise on commit time. On this machine that capped one team at about 400 redemptions/s, and the p99 rose to 277 ms. Load spread across teams did not show it. Reproduce, against a throwaway PostgreSQL 18 and NATS (the CI workflow ci governed scale.yml runs the same nightly and on dispatch, and uploads the report): ELITEA GOVERNED SCALE TEAMS , APPS , AGENTS and GRANTS change the dimensions, REDEEMS the spread redeem count, and ELITEA GOVERNED SCALE REPORT writes the report to a file. Turning it off Turning the flag off stops new governed admissions. Runs already pinned stay governed, and their continuations still go out on the governed subjects. The chart turns the worker's governed lane off with the flag, so set worker.governedContext: "true" until those runs have drained, then remove it. Such a run fails closed at its next credential use ( UNIMPLEMENTED ) instead of falling back to legacy behaviour. To drain without failures, wait until no governed run is active before turning the flag off. Rolling back to an earlier release is refused by its migration runner when the database holds a migration the release does not know. Turn the flag off instead. The runbook lists the checks. Conformance A conformance suite checks the governed profile end to end on the standalone stack: It uses the test only overlay deploy/docker compose.governed.yml . The overlay adds OpenBao (TLS, KV v2 with cas required , JWT auth) and test doubles for Jira, SharePoint/Graph, Entra and the inbound MCP token issuer. No chart references it. The script takes one stack through five phases in this order: 1. Flag off. 2. Flag on. 3. Flag on, with a worker that has no governed context. 4. The governed worker restored. 5. Flag off again (rollback). It runs cases GOV 001 to GOV 010 and the rollback test, and checks every skip against scripts/go/declared skips.txt . Every credential the suite creates is a unique canary value. At the end the script scans for those values in: The NATS traffic. A dump of every database. Every container log, including the OpenTelemetry export. The audit outbox. Any match fails the run. The scanner first tests itself on a planted leak. conformance/governed/EVIDENCE.md maps each acceptance line to a case or unit test, or to the gate that defers it. CI runs the suite nightly, on demand, and on pull requests that change the suite or its stack ( ci governed conformance.yml ).

title: Deploy from scratch
text: This page takes an empty Kubernetes cluster to a working Elitea deployment with single sign on, chat, agents, indexing and shared models. Follow it top to bottom, once. It covers the same install as Install with Helm, but in full: what to decide first, the secrets and certificate authorities the chart expects, and the edge in front of the platform. When you are done, GitOps with ArgoCD shows how to keep the same install in git. It targets the one chart layout: a release whose docs/UPGRADING.md has the entry "One chart: NATS bundled". NATS JetStream and its stream bootstrap are part of the elitea chart; earlier releases installed them from two separate charts, nats and nats bootstrap , which are no longer published. A values file or a guide that still mentions those charts, runtimeRedis , worker.implementation: python or Redis passwords is out of date, and the chart refuses most of it. Installing on Google Cloud? Read Deploy on Google Cloud (GKE) alongside this page. It covers Cloud SQL, a GCS bucket without keys, the edge on GKE, and platform models authenticated by a service account. Deploy on GKE with Argo CD is the same install as one Argo CD Application, with secrets from Google Secret Manager. What you end up with | Component | Comes from | Notes | | | | | | elitea main, elitea web, elitea scheduler, elitea llm gateway, elitea worker, elitea vector, Qdrant, OTel collector | the elitea chart | one release, one values file, one version | | NATS JetStream and its streams | the elitea chart ( nats , natsBootstrap ) | bundled and on by default; same release, same namespace | | PostgreSQL 16+ | you | an existing server, a managed service, or an operator such as CloudNativePG | | S3 compatible bucket (or Azure Blob, GCS) | you | must exist before the first install | | cert manager | you | issues every in cluster mTLS certificate | | Ingress controller or Gateway API implementation, public TLS certificate, DNS | you | the public edge, one route to elitea main; see The edge | | OIDC identity provider (and optionally SAML, SCIM) | you | Keycloak, Entra ID, Okta, Dex, Google... | | Model providers | you | OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Gemini, or a self hosted OpenAI compatible server | Every first party image and chart is public on ghcr.io/elitea ng , so no image pull secret is needed. The worker and the DeepWiki and Inventory pods reach elitea main over gRPC on a private mTLS listener (port 9446) that elitea main serves itself, admitting only clients with a certificate from the runtime CA, and each gRPC service on it only the workload identities configured for it. It serves no HTTP; check it with gRPC health, not an HTTP probe. There is no internal proxy to run. In front, elitea main is the browser edge too: it relays /app and /docs to elitea web and serves its MCP endpoint itself, so your public edge needs exactly one route, / to elitea main. Any Ingress controller or Gateway API implementation does, the managed GKE Ingress and Gateway included. See The edge. Before you start: decide these Write the answers down. Every one ends up in a value or a Secret, and several are hard to change later. | Decision | Example | Where it goes | Changing it later | | | | | | | Public hostname | elitea.example.com | DEPLOYMENT URL , OIDC redirect URI, gateway self origins, the edge route | edit values, re register the redirect URI | | Namespace | elitea | everything; NATS and its bootstrap are in the same release | reinstall | | Chart version | the latest release | version on the one chart | upgrade (read docs/UPGRADING.md first) | | PostgreSQL server and its max connections | pg.internal:5432 , 200 | the database DSN Secrets, postgresql.maxConnections | edit values; the chart re checks the connection budget | | Bucket and region | elitea artifacts , eu west 1 | STORAGE / S3 env | data does not move by itself | | Identity provider and client | issuer URL, client id, client secret | OIDC env and a Secret | edit values | | First administrator | email:admin@example.com | ELITEA INITIAL GLOBAL ADMINS | add entries any time; nobody is ever demoted by this list | | Worker identity (SPIFFE id) | spiffe://elitea.example.com/ns/elitea/sa/worker | the worker certificate, worker.runtimeSession.expectedIdentity | re mint the worker certificate | | Model provider hosts | api.openai.com , 10.0.5.20:8000 | GATEWAY EGRESS ALLOWLIST | edit values | Prerequisites A cluster whose CNI enforces NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium, and similar). The chart renders default deny ingress policies and relies on them. kubectl and helm : Helm 4.3 or newer is recommended, and Helm 3.8 or newer (the first that pulls OCI charts) also works. Installed cluster wide before anything else. The bundled NATS, the LLM gateway, elitea vector and the NATS client identities all render cert manager Certificate objects. The agent state migrations use SQL/JSON syntax introduced in 16. No extension is needed: every vector is kept in Qdrant through elitea vector, not in PostgreSQL. S3 compatible (AWS S3, MinIO, RustFS, Ceph RGW), Azure Blob or GCS. There is no local disk backend. An Ingress controller, or a Gateway API implementation with a Gateway that terminates TLS for your hostname. It needs one route, / to elitea main, that keeps long streams open. A confidential client with the redirect URI https:// /auth/oidc/callback . For GitHub, which has no OIDC sign in, put Dex in front of it. Capacity The worker dominates. The figures below are requests for the install on this page. Limits are higher. | Component | Replicas | CPU request | Memory request | Storage | | | | | | | | elitea main | 2 (HPA to 3) | 100m | 256Mi | — | | elitea web | 2 | 10m | 32Mi | — | | elitea scheduler | 1 | 50m | 64Mi | — | | elitea llm gateway | 1 | 250m | 1Gi | — | | elitea worker | 1 | 2 | 4Gi | — | | elitea vector | 2 | 250m | 128Mi | — | | Qdrant | 1 (3 for HA) | 500m | 2Gi | 50Gi PVC | | OTel collector | 1 | 50m | 128Mi | — | | NATS (bundled, one node) | 1 (3 for HA) | 100m | 256Mi | 10Gi PVC | Plan for about 4 CPU and 10Gi of memory in requests, and at least one node with 2 free CPUs for the worker during a rolling update. Step 1: Namespace and certificate authorities Three private certificate authorities protect the in cluster hops. None of them is your public certificate, and they must stay separate: | Issuer | Signs | Created by | | | | | | elitea nats ca | NATS server and every NATS client identity | the elitea chart, automatically | | elitea internal ca | the elitea main → LLM gateway mTLS hop | you , below | | elitea runtime ca | elitea vector certificates. It must be the same CA as the runtime material you mint in Step 4 | you , below, from that material | Apply the internal CA. cert manager generates its key and nothing leaves the cluster: The chart's defaults name ClusterIssuer s. The values in Step 6 switch both references to these namespaced Issuer s, which read their CA from the platform's own namespace and need no access to cert manager's namespace. Anyone allowed to create a cert manager Certificate or read Secrets in this namespace can mint a NATS or runtime identity. Limit those RBAC rights to the deployer and operators. Step 2: PostgreSQL The platform needs one login role and two databases , both owned by that role: | Database | Holds | Read by | | | | | | elitea v2 (the platform database) | every platform schema ( centry , p per project, elitea auth , elitea runtime , gateway , ...) | elitea main, its migration Job, the scheduler, the LLM gateway, the workload session Job | | elitea v2 agentstate | agent sessions and graph checkpoints | the worker, the agent state migration Job | The migration Job runs as the role and creates every schema itself, so the role needs ownership of the platform database and no superuser rights. Nothing is imported: the platform starts empty apart from what the migrations seed. Run once as an administrator: Then keep the chart's database preparation hook off, and say that the databases exist: Without externallyManaged: true the chart refuses to render. Otherwise the install would look healthy and then fail every agent turn with "The durable agent checkpoint store is unavailable". Create the role and the platform database yourself as above. Then let the dbInit hook create the agent state database before each install and upgrade. It needs an administrator DSN with the CREATE DATABASE right for the platform database : With CloudNativePG, a Cluster with enableSuperuserAccess: true publishes a Secret of this shape. Point dbInit.database.existingSecret at it. TLS. Put sslmode=require in both DSNs. The chart has no mount for a server CA bundle, so verify full is not available yet. The DSN is a plain libpq URL. Generate the password URL safe, as the Step 4 script does: a / or + in it breaks URL parsing, and the error then names a host or port instead of the password. The connection budget PostgreSQL connections run out before CPU does. With the runtime plane on, each elitea main replica opens one primary pool of 6 plus six isolated runtime pools totalling 36, and elitea vector's introspection pool adds 2: 44 connections per replica . The chart adds up every component at its replica ceiling (elitea main, the gateway, the scheduler, DeepWiki, Inventory and the worker's agent state pool: 216 more with every autoscaler at its default ceiling) and refuses to render when the total exceeds postgresql.maxConnections reservedConnections . The reserve covers the Jobs, backups and interactive psql . Scaling has the formula per component. | max connections on the server | reservedConnections | Largest main.autoscaling.maxReplicas (other components at their defaults) | | | | | | 200 | 25 | 2 | | 300 | 25 | 4 | | 600 (the chart's default) | 25 | 10 | Read the real value with SHOW max connections; . The chart cannot read it, so it believes the number in postgresql.maxConnections . A transaction mode PgBouncer is shipped with the chart ( pgbouncer.enabled ) when you need more elitea main replicas than the server can hold. Point elitea main db at the pooler's Service when you turn it on. Step 3: Object storage Create the bucket before the first install . elitea main's readiness probe tolerates a missing bucket. The boot step right after it does not: it writes the bucket's lifecycle rule. So with no bucket, the release reports success and elitea main then crash loops. The credential elitea main uses needs: s3:GetObject , s3:PutObject , s3:DeleteObject , s3:ListBucket s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration . elitea main writes the rule elitea abort incomplete multipart uploads and replaces the bucket's whole lifecycle configuration . Use a dedicated bucket. s3:GetEncryptionConfiguration . Without it the platform still starts, but the cloud executor handoff stays off. On AWS with IRSA, or on any cloud with workload identity, skip the Secret, remove the two S3 entries from main.secrets in Step 6, and annotate main.serviceAccount . For a self hosted MinIO, RustFS or Ceph that you administer, objectInit.enabled: true creates the bucket from the same Secret. Azure Blob and GCS use STORAGE BACKEND: azure or gcs with their own variables. For GCS with Workload Identity, which needs no Secret, see Deploy on Google Cloud. Uploads up to 150 MiB are accepted by default ( ARTIFACT MAX OBJECT BYTES ). Step 4: Mint the secrets Nothing secret belongs in a values file: a Helm value renders into a ConfigMap. The chart only takes names of Secrets you create. Generate the material The script below writes every generated value into ./elitea material , owner only. It needs OpenSSL 3, which is what produces the Ed25519 key. Keep the directory somewhere safe and out of git . Losing secrets master key makes every stored credential unreadable. Use the generated db password when you create the role in Step 2. Create the Secrets The key names are part of the contract. The chart and the binaries look files up by these exact names, and nothing renames them for you. What each Secret is | Secret | Keys | Read by | Rules | | | | | | | elitea main db | database url | main, migrations, scheduler, gateway, workload session Job | DSN of the platform database | | elitea llm gateway secrets | identity secret , secrets master key | gateway; main also reads secrets master key from here | the master key wraps every project's vault key. Never rotate it casually : a new key cannot read what the old one wrote | | elitea main llm gateway secrets | gateway identity secret | main | same value as identity secret above, or every /llm call fails | | elitea main sso | application secret key , oidc client secret | main | elitea main refuses to start with single sign on configured and no application secret key | | elitea main storage secrets | s3 access key , s3 secret key | main, objectInit | omit when using workload identity | | elitea main auth material | auth attempt key , auth pat signing key , auth form users.json | main | the three must hold different bytes. Rotating the PAT key invalidates every personal access token | | elitea runtime material | runtime CA, Ed25519 private key, keyring, three listener keypairs | main | the keyring's key id must equal main.runtime.signingKeyId | | elitea worker material | runtime CA, worker client keypair, keyring, spool key, agent state DSN | worker, agent state migration Job, workload session Job | same CA and keyring as the runtime material | | elitea runtime ca | tls.crt , tls.key | the elitea runtime ca Issuer | the runtime CA itself | | elitea qdrant api | api key | elitea vector, Qdrant | generate once; a value that changes on every sync locks elitea vector out | | elitea deepwiki secrets | identity secret | main, DeepWiki | signs and verifies the identity headers elitea main sends DeepWiki | | elitea inventory secrets | identity secret | main, Inventory | the same, for Inventory; a different value from DeepWiki's | Every name above is the chart's fixed default, so the values file names none of them. The chart creates the remaining certificate Secrets itself through cert manager. These include the NATS client certificates, the gateway server and client certificates, the elitea vector certificates, Qdrant's TLS certificate ( elitea qdrant tls ) and the DeepWiki and Inventory callback client certificates ( elitea deepwiki callback client , elitea inventory callback client , one DNS SAN elitea subapp callback , from the elitea runtime ca Issuer). Scripts written before 4.7 also mint redis passwords, a Redis server keypair, a redis users.acl file and an elitea runtime redis material Secret. Nothing reads any of them now; drop them. Scripts written before the platform listener ( 1359) also mint a platform edge keypair and an elitea platform edge tls Secret, and set worker.platformEdge ; delete all three. Scripts from the first platform listener release also mint a main platform client keypair; elitea main no longer reads it, so drop it. The redis auth password and runtime ca.crt keys in the auth material Secret are ignored too. If your old script put the master key in a separate elitea secrets master Secret, either keep it there and point both main.secrets.SECRETS MASTER KEY and llmGateway.secrets.SECRETS MASTER KEY at it, or move it. Two different keys would put two incompatible formats in one table. Step 5: NATS NATS is the platform's bus for live updates, presence, LLM budget counters and the runtime command bus. It runs mTLS only, with one account per plane, and it is part of the elitea release : there is nothing to install separately. The chart renders the server (the upstream NATS chart, a pinned dependency that the published chart carries), its CA ( elitea nats ca ), its certificates, a NetworkPolicy that admits port 4222 only from the platform's NATS clients, and the elitea nats bootstrap hook Job that creates every stream, KV bucket and durable consumer. elitea main refuses to start until they exist; until the Job has run, it restarts and then settles. The defaults are one node with JetStream on a 10Gi volume. To change them, set the upstream chart's values under nats in your values file: For three nodes, layer the chart's values nats ha.yaml ( f values nats ha.yaml f values prod.yaml , so the storage settings in your own file still win). It sets the bootstrap's replica count ( natsBootstrap.replicas ) to 3 as well; the chart refuses a bootstrap whose replica count does not match the cluster. Step 6: Write the values file This is a complete production values file for the install on this page. Every elitea.example.com and every value in angle brackets is yours to replace. The chart checks the combinations while it renders and names the field when something is missing or contradictory. Choices in this file you may want to change The chart refuses to render until you choose. With allowlist , the gateway calls only the hosts in GATEWAY EGRESS ALLOWLIST , and governance rows added later can only extend that list. With public unrestricted , any public host is allowed until the first governance row narrows it. In both modes a private address is reachable only through an entry that names it, by IP or CIDR with an optional port (for example 10.0.5.20:8000 ). A host name alone never opens a private address. For a self hosted vLLM or Ollama, list its address and port. ELITEA ALLOW PROJECT OWN LLMS: "false" limits every project to the models an administrator shares from the public project. Use it for a public or demo deployment, where a project credential could otherwise point anywhere the allowlist permits. The value must be exactly "true" or "false" . Toolkit connection checks, MCP servers, MCP OAuth and webhooks have their own allowlists on elitea main ( ELITEA TOOLKIT CHECK ALLOWLIST , ELITEA MCP EGRESS ALLOWLIST , ELITEA MCP OAUTH EGRESS ALLOWLIST , ELITEA WEBHOOK EGRESS ALLOWLIST ). Their defaults refuse every private address. To reach a self hosted GitLab, Jira or MCP server on a private network, list both its name and its range, for example gitlab.corp.example,10.20.0.0/16 . The worker's index runs reach a default set of public SaaS hosts (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps, Figma, Zephyr and Xray cloud). Self hosted sources need worker.runtime.indexEgressAllowlist . PDF and Office extraction needs worker.extractor.enabled: true , which adds a sidecar of about 2.5Gi to the worker pod. Without it, those files are skipped as unsupported. Optional components The values above install the platform with every default on: the runtime plane, the worker, elitea vector with Qdrant, DeepWiki and Inventory. Each of those is one switch ( main.runtime.enabled , worker.enabled , vector.enabled with qdrant.enabled , deepwiki.enabled , inventory.enabled ); set it to false to leave the feature out, and the render tells you if another feature still needs it. The components below are off by default. Turn each one on after the base install works, one at a time, and render after each change. | Component | What it adds | Turn it on when | | | | | | Document extractor ( worker.extractor ) | PDF and Office text extraction, as a sidecar of about 2.5Gi in the worker pod | users index or attach PDF, Word, Excel or PowerPoint files. Without it, those files are skipped as unsupported | | Cloud executor ( sandboxKubernetes ) | agent workspaces run in gVisor isolated pods in a separate namespace | users choose Send to cloud | | Egress proxy ( egressProxy ) | per project host allowlists for cloud executor workspaces | you run the cloud executor and projects restrict its network to named hosts | | PgBouncer ( pgbouncer ) | a transaction mode pooler in front of elitea main | you need more elitea main replicas than max connections allows | The egress proxy's audit certificate defaults to a cert manager ClusterIssuer , as do DeepWiki's and Inventory's (the values file above already overrides those). This guide creates namespaced Issuer s in Step 1, so set kind: Issuer in each component's issuerRef . Otherwise the certificates never issue, and the pods wait for their Secrets forever. It needs the indexing runtime, which the values above already turn on. No Secret is needed. DeepWiki and Inventory are on by default, and the values file above sets everything they need: the git allowlists and the namespaced Issuers. Each one is a separate Deployment that elitea main calls over mTLS. It writes its own schema ( deepwiki build , inventory graph ) into the platform database. The database owner from Step 2 already has the rights it needs. Their dense vectors go to elitea vector, so vector.enabled: false beside either one fails the render. From deepwiki.enabled and inventory.enabled the chart derives elitea main's side: ELITEA DEEPWIKI ENABLED / ELITEA INVENTORY ENABLED , the git allowlists (copied from the provider's env ), the client certificate paths and their mounts ( main.fileConfig.deepwikiClientMaterial / inventoryClientMaterial , issued by the chart), and ELITEA DEEPWIKI PLATFORM GRPC TARGET / ELITEA INVENTORY PLATFORM GRPC TARGET ( elitea grpc:9443 , a headless Service that elitea main balances over with round robin ; the certificate is still checked against elitea svc ). A main.env value that agrees is kept; one that disagrees fails the render. The old BASE URL keys are refused. A provider with more than one replica also needs its NATS client certificate ( elitea deepwiki / elitea inventory , issued by the chart when NATS TLS is on) so a cancel reaches the replica running the job. The providers call elitea main only over gRPC on its private listener (port 9446): the engines' model calls ( elitea.llm.v1.ModelService ), artifact uploads and reads from both containers ( elitea.runtime.v1.ArtifactObjectService ), and Inventory's investigate source tool calls ( elitea.runtime.v1.InternalToolService ). So DeepWiki and Inventory need the runtime plane ( main.runtime.enabled ), and their callback client certificates, which the chart issues from the elitea runtime ca Issuer. The chart mounts those and the runtime CA into both containers of each provider pod, sets ELITEA DEEPWIKI ARTIFACT SERVICE URL and ELITEA DEEPWIKI MODEL SERVICE URL (and the ELITEA INVENTORY pair) to https://elitea main:9446 , and adds dns:elitea subapp callback to the identities elitea main admits for each service. No provider pod reaches elitea main on port 8080. The old ELITEA DEEPWIKI CALLBACK BASE URL and ELITEA INVENTORY CALLBACK BASE URL keys and deepwiki.callbackViaPlatformListener are refused. To bring your own callback certificate instead, set callbackClient.certManager.enabled: false and create the Secret ( tls.crt , tls.key , one DNS SAN elitea subapp callback , signed by the runtime CA). Follow Cloud executor on Kubernetes. It mints the sandbox material, creates the run token key pair for the egress proxy, and gives the full values. The egress proxy is needed only for cloud executor workspaces whose project limits network access to named hosts. A NetworkPolicy cannot match host names, so those workspaces reach the internet only through the proxy, with a run token signed by elitea main. If it is off, a turn in such a project is refused with workspace run.egress proxy unavailable , and its network access is never widened instead. The proxy does not affect the LLM gateway, toolkits or the worker. Those have their own allowlists, described in the accordions above. The chart refuses egressProxy.enabled without both key Secrets, with the same Secret used for both, with fewer than 2 replicas, or without the execution namespace and your cluster's pod and service CIDRs. Only elitea main's pods go through the pooler. The migration Job, dbInit , the scheduler and the gateway keep the direct DSN in elitea main db . The database name in the pooled DSN must equal pgbouncer.database . Render it before you install it Each refusal names the field and tells you what to do. Fix them all here, where they cost nothing. Install Do not add wait to this first install: the NATS bootstrap is a post install hook, so wait would wait for workloads that wait for the streams the hook creates. With Helm 4, atomic is spelled rollback on failure . The hooks run in a fixed order: the database preparation (when on), then the platform and agent state migrations, then the workload session row. Then the Deployments and the NATS StatefulSet roll out, and the elitea nats bootstrap Job creates the streams. elitea main can restart a few times while cert manager issues its NATS and gateway certificates and until the bootstrap has run; that settles by itself. Watch it with: Step 7: The edge elitea main is the browser edge. It serves the API, redirects / to /app/ , relays /app and /docs to elitea web, and serves its MCP endpoint ( /app/ /mcp ) and icon files under /app itself. So the public edge is one route: / to elitea main:8080 . No rule names elitea web, and none needs a regular expression. What the edge must do 1. Send / to elitea main , port 8080, and nothing to elitea web directly. Its NetworkPolicy admits elitea main only. 2. Keep streams open. Chat, the events stream, /llm and MCP tools/call are server sent events, and a model answer can stream for several minutes. elitea main writes a comment into an idle stream every 25 seconds, so an idle timeout above 60 seconds is enough; disable the per request timeout and turn off response buffering. /llm/v1/realtime needs WebSocket upgrades. 3. Accept large uploads , at least 150 MiB, or whatever ARTIFACT MAX OBJECT BYTES is set to. You do not need to strip identity headers or hide /readyz and /startupz : elitea main deletes client supplied identity headers itself before any route runs, and answers the two probe paths to a loopback caller only (its probes run inside the container). The route Let the chart render it: main.ingress.enabled: true renders an Ingress, or, with gatewayApi: true , an HTTPRoute, each a single / rule to elitea main. The chart's HTTPRoute also removes the client identity headers ( main.ingress.stripIdentityHeaders ), as defence in depth. It sets no timeout, so raise your implementation's route and idle timeouts where it has them. For a route that has to live with the Gateway rather than with the release, apply the reviewed copy in deploy/gateway api/httproute.yaml after adding your parentRefs and hostnames ; you can add timeouts: {request: 0s} to its rule there. Set your controller's read timeout and body size limit through main.ingress.annotations (on ingress nginx, nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy read timeout , proxy send timeout , proxy buffering: "off" and proxy body size ). The chart adds the BackendConfig ( timeoutSec: 3600 , a /healthz health check, connection draining, an optional Cloud Armor policy) and the FrontendConfig (HTTPS redirect) the Google load balancer needs. There are no ingress pods, so the NetworkPolicy must admit Google's ranges; see Deploy on GKE with Argo CD. Admit the edge through the NetworkPolicy networkPolicies.main.ingressFrom in the values file must select the pods that actually forward traffic, meaning your gateway's or ingress controller's data plane pods, not its controller. Find their namespace and labels: If the selector is wrong, the gateway gets connection timeouts from elitea main while everything in the namespace looks healthy. A cloud load balancer with no pods (the GKE Ingress, container native) is admitted by ipBlock instead: 35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22 on GKE. Step 8: First sign in, the public project and models 1. Register the redirect URI https://elitea.example.com/auth/oidc/callback with the identity provider. The provider must issue an email claim. 2. Sign in at https://elitea.example.com/ as the account named in ELITEA INITIAL GLOBAL ADMINS . That account becomes an administrator during the sign in, and nothing needs to be run by hand. Your personal project and an auto issued personal access token are created in the same step. The worker needs that token to act for you in chat. email: matches only when the identity provider marks the address verified ( email verified: true ). oidc: always matches. After a first sign in, open Settings › Profile and copy the Sign in reference row. Add it, and sign in again. The list never demotes anybody. Remove administrators in the admin console instead. 3. Check the public project. The first migration seeds project 1 , "Default Project", which platform.aiProjectId: "1" names. Its shared models are what every other project can use. Keep it, or name another existing project. The chart refuses a values file in which the copies of this id disagree. 4. Add a model provider. In the admin console ( /admin/app ), go to Configuration › LLM Proxy › Providers & models . Add a credential for OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Vertex AI, Amazon Bedrock, EPAM AI DIAL or an OpenAI compatible server (vLLM, Ollama). Then publish the models you want shared, and choose the platform default model on the same tab. LLM Proxy has the details. A provider whose host is not in GATEWAY EGRESS ALLOWLIST is refused at request time. On GKE, Vertex AI and AI DIAL can authenticate as the gateway's Google service account instead of with a key; see Platform models with a service account. 5. Optional: SAML and SCIM. SAML providers are configured only in the admin console ( Configuration › Authentication ), so sign in through OIDC first. Because OIDC is configured in the values file, the sign in routes already exist, and a SAML provider added later needs no restart. Give the identity provider the metadata URL https://elitea.example.com/auth/saml/metadata . SCIM accepts only a SCIM client credential created on the same page; personal access tokens are refused there. Bind directory groups to a project and a role on the same page. Authentication describes every field. Then open a chat, pick a shared model and send a message. That one exchange exercises the edge, elitea main, NATS, the command bus, the worker, the platform listener, the agent state database, the LLM gateway and the provider. Step 9: Verify https://elitea.example.com/app/ and https://elitea.example.com/admin/app , signed in as the administrator. GET /api/v2/admin/gateway/status as an administrator reports the egress allowlist and whether rate limits are enforceable. The latter needs NATS. The test that matters. If it hangs or fails, use the table below. When it does not work | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | | | | | | helm template refuses | a missing or contradictory value | the message names the field; fix it there | | elitea main CrashLoopBackOff right after a green install | the bucket does not exist, or the credential cannot set its lifecycle rule | create the bucket; grant s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration | | elitea main exits naming the presence bucket or NATS | the elitea nats bootstrap hook Job has not succeeded yet, or natsBootstrap.enabled is off | wait for the Job and read its logs;
