Index data from a source for source specific setup fields. Schedule re indexing to keep an index current automatically.

title: Index and search data with tools
text: Indexing tools aren't limited to the Indexes tab — once a toolkit has an index, an agent, a pipeline, or a chat conversation with that toolkit attached can call its search tools directly. The tools | Tool | What it does | Where it can run | | | | | | Index Data | Creates or updates an index | Indexes tab only | | Search Index | Direct semantic search over an index | Indexes tab, chat, agents, pipelines, Test tools | | Stepback Search Index | Rewrites the query before searching, for better recall on complex questions | Same as Search Index | | Stepback Summary Index | Runs a stepback search and returns a generated summary | Same as Search Index | | Remove Index | Deletes an index | Indexes tab only | | List Indexes | Lists a toolkit's indexes | Rarely needed — the Indexes tab already lists them | Index Data can't be tested from the Test tools pane. The Go backend routes indexing through a separate, asynchronous endpoint owned by the Indexes tab. If you press Run on Index Data from a toolkit's Test tools pane, you get that route's own refusal rather than a result — use the Indexes tab to actually create or update an index. Search from chat or an agent 1. Add the indexed toolkit as a participant in a conversation, or attach it to an agent. 2. Make sure the search tool you want (Search Index, Stepback Search Index, or Stepback Summary Index) is turned on in the toolkit's configuration. 3. Ask a question in natural language. The toolkit runs the search tool against the index and returns matching content — or, with Stepback Summary Index, a generated summary of it. Search from the Indexes tab You can also run these search tools directly from an index's own page, without going through chat — useful for quickly checking what an index actually returns before wiring it into an agent. Vector store and embeddings Search quality depends on the embedding model indexing itself uses: it turns your query into a vector, which is compared with the indexed vectors in the platform's vector store (Qdrant, behind the elitea vector service). There is no vector store configuration to set up. See Index external data for how to configure the embedding model. Next steps Use the Indexes tab to create an index in the first place. Schedule re indexing to keep results current.

title: Schedule re-indexing
text: Scheduled reindexing keeps an index synchronized with its source automatically, instead of you having to reindex by hand every time the underlying content changes. Before you schedule The index must already exist and be in a usable state — Completed or Partially Indexed . An index in Failed or Stopped state needs a successful reindex first. If the toolkit requires credentials for the scheduled run, you'll need one available: private credentials in a personal project, project credentials in a team project. Set a schedule 1. Open the index's page from the toolkit's Indexes tab. 2. In the Schedule section, select + Schedule if none exists yet, or the edit icon on an existing schedule. 3. Choose a cron expression — either with the visual builder or by typing one directly (format: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week). 4. If the toolkit needs credentials for the scheduled run, pick one from the dropdown. 5. Save. The schedule shows its next run time, and you can turn it on or off later without losing the configured expression. Each schedule belongs to one index. You can turn it off temporarily with the toggle, or delete it with the edit panel's delete icon, without affecting the index's data. Notifications and history A scheduled reindex raises a notification when it completes, just like a manual one — see Notifications. Scheduled runs also appear in the index's history alongside manual reindexes, so you can confirm a schedule actually ran. Next steps Use the Indexes tab for the full index lifecycle. Index data from a source for source specific setup. This page could not verify from source whether a scheduled reindex only pulls changes since the last run or reprocesses the source in full each time — check your deployment's behavior before relying on a tight schedule for a large, frequently changing source.

title: Use the Indexes tab
text: Every toolkit type that supports indexing shows an Indexes tab next to its Configuration tab. This page walks through the full lifecycle: create, monitor, reindex, schedule, and review history. Before you start, confirm your project has an embedding model (Settings › AI Providers), and that the toolkit's Index Data tool is turned on. Without these, the tab shows an explanation instead of the create index form — see Index external data. Create an index 1. Open a toolkit that supports indexing and switch to its Indexes tab. 2. Start a new index. Give it a unique name (it can't be changed later) and set the toolkit specific scope fields — for example a repository and branch for GitHub, or a space key for Confluence. See Index data from a source for the fields each source needs. 3. Optionally turn off "skip unsupported extensions" if you want files with uncommon extensions indexed as plain text instead of skipped. 4. Start the run and watch its progress. The index reaches Completed when everything indexed cleanly, or Partially Indexed when some files were skipped (both states are fully searchable). An index in Failed or Stopped state did not complete and needs another run before it's usable. Manage an existing index Opening an index from its card gives you a Configuration view (the index's own settings — everything except its name is editable) and a history view. From there you can: Reindex — pick up new and changed content from the source. Unchanged files aren't reprocessed; the previous working index stays searchable until the new run finishes successfully. Schedule — see Schedule re indexing. Delete — permanently remove the index and its data. Only available when the toolkit's Remove Index tool is turned on. Review index history The index's history view lists every past run — the initial index, manual reindexes, and scheduled reindexes — in order, with status and file counts for each. Use it to confirm a scheduled reindex actually ran, or to see when an index last failed. Notifications Indexing operations (initial runs and reindexes) raise a notification when they finish, whether they succeed, partially succeed, or fail. See Notifications for how to review these. Next steps Index and search data with tools to run search against a completed index from chat or an agent. Schedule re indexing to keep an index current automatically.

title: Use the flow editor
text: The flow editor is the visual workspace for building a pipeline: a canvas you arrange nodes on, connected by the edges the pipeline follows at runtime. Open the flow editor Open Pipelines , then an existing pipeline or a new one, and select Flow in its Configuration tab (next to YAML ). Both views describe the same pipeline and stay in sync — a change in one shows up in the other. Add and connect a node Click the + button on the canvas to open the Add node menu. Choose from the nine types the runtime executes: Agent, Decision, HITL, LLM, MCP, Printer, Router, State modifier, Toolkit. See Pipeline node types for what each does. Click the new node to open its configuration panel and set its fields (model, toolkit, routing condition, and so on, depending on the type). Drag from one node's connection point to the next to create an edge. You can also start a connection and drop it on empty canvas to add a new node in the same step. Code and Custom node types are not offered in the Add node menu — the runtime has no execution logic for either. A pipeline authored before this restriction that still contains one keeps displaying it, but you cannot add a new one. Canvas controls The left side toolbar zooms in and out, fits the whole pipeline to view, locks the canvas against accidental edits, collapses or expands all node cards at once, and auto arranges the layout. Guides and references Pipeline structure: entry point, states and connections Edit a pipeline as YAML Pipeline node types

title: Control-flow nodes: decision, router and state
text: Control flow nodes decide what happens next, or reshape the pipeline's state without calling an external service. Router Evaluates a template condition (Jinja style) against the pipeline's state and picks one of several named routes, with a default fallback if nothing matches. | Field | What it does | | | | | Condition | A template that resolves to one of your route names — for example, branching on whether a state variable contains "approved" | | Routes | The node IDs the condition can resolve to; route names must exactly match a node ID, case sensitively | | Default output | Where to go if the condition resolves to nothing recognized | Router is fast and deterministic — no model call — best when the branching logic is an explicit rule. Decision Uses an LLM to pick a route based on a natural language description, instead of a template rule. Best for routing that depends on interpreting meaning rather than matching a fixed pattern. | Field | What it does | | | | | Description | Plain language instructions telling the model how to choose between routes | | Decision outputs | The node IDs the model can choose from | | Default output | Fallback route if the model can't decide confidently | Decision nodes are slower than Router (they make a model call) and cannot connect directly to another Decision node — put a Router, LLM, or Toolkit node between two decisions if you need a second one in sequence. State modifier Reshapes the pipeline's state without calling a model or a tool: combine values, format text, do simple arithmetic, or clear out variables you no longer need. | Field | What it does | | | | | Template | A Jinja style template referencing input variables — for example, Hello, {{ user name }}! | | Input | The state variables the template is allowed to read | | Output | Where the rendered result is written | | Variables to clean | Optional list of variables to reset afterward (strings to "" , lists to [] , numbers to 0 ) | Guides and references Pipeline node types Interaction nodes: HITL and printer Execution nodes: LLM, agent, toolkit, MCP Pipeline structure: entry point, state and connections

title: Execution nodes: LLM, agent, toolkit and MCP
text: Execution nodes are where a pipeline does its work — calling a model, delegating to an agent, or running a specific tool with known parameters. LLM Calls a model directly with a system message and a task, without wrapping it in a full agent. Useful when you know exactly what you want asked and don't need an agent's own toolkits or persona. | Field | What it does | | | | | System | Fixed text, a template, or a state variable — sets the model's role/behavior | | Task | The request sent to the model, same three input types | | Chat history | What prior conversation context (if any) to include | | Input / Output | Which state variables feed in, and which are populated from the response | | Toolkits | Toolkits or MCPs the model can call as tools during this step | | Structured output | When enabled, the response is parsed into your named output variables instead of dropped into messages as free text | Agent Delegates the step to an agent you've already added to the pipeline (Pipeline Configuration › Toolkits), reusing its instructions, model and attached toolkits instead of reconfiguring an LLM call from scratch. | Field | What it does | | | | | Agent | Which added agent runs this step | | Task | The instruction sent to the agent — fixed, templated, or from state | | Input / Output | Same pattern as the LLM node | | Custom variables | Values for any custom variables the agent's own configuration defines | Toolkit Calls one specific tool from a toolkit already attached to the pipeline, with parameters mapped directly from state — no LLM call, fast and deterministic. | Field | What it does | | | | | Toolkit / Tool | Which attached toolkit, and which of its tools to run | | Input mapping | Maps each of the tool's parameters to a fixed value, a template, or a state variable | | Output | Where the tool's result is written | MCP Calls one tool from a connected MCP server, the same way the Toolkit node calls a toolkit tool — direct parameter mapping, no LLM step. MCP nodes only reach MCP servers; for an Elitea toolkit's own tools, use the Toolkit node instead. | Field | What it does | | | | | MCP server / Tool | Which connected MCP server and which of its tools | | Input mapping | Maps the tool's parameters, same as the Toolkit node | | Structured output | Parse the tool's result into named state variables instead of messages | Guides and references Pipeline node types Interaction nodes: HITL and printer Control flow nodes: decision, router and state Use credentials

title: Interaction nodes: human-in-the-loop and printer
text: Interaction nodes are where a pipeline talks to a person, either to ask for a decision or to hand back a formatted result. Human in the loop (HITL) A HITL node pauses the pipeline and waits for a person to respond with one of three actions, each routable to a different next node: | Action | Typical use | | | | | Approve | Continue down the main path | | Edit | Send a modified value back into the pipeline before continuing — this needs a state key configured to receive the edit | | Reject | Stop or divert to a different path | Connect each action to whichever node should run next; an action with no route configured has nowhere to go. A HITL node is how you build an explicit approval step into a pipeline's own logic — distinct from the guardrail confirmation prompt that can appear in chat before a sensitive tool call, which is triggered by admin configuration rather than a node you place yourself. See Require confirmation for sensitive actions for that related flow. Printer A Printer node formats a final message and writes it to the pipeline's output — typically the last node before END in a path that should show something back to the user. It takes the content you want printed (which can reference earlier state) and stores it in the reserved printer output state key. Because printer output is a reserved state key, don't reuse it for anything else in the same pipeline — a later node that overwrites it silently replaces whatever the Printer node produced. See Pipeline structure for the full list of reserved keys. Guides and references Pipeline structure: entry point, states and connections Execution nodes: LLM, agent, toolkit and MCP Control flow nodes: decision, router and state

title: Pipeline node types
text: The flow editor lets you drop more node types onto the canvas than the runtime actually executes. Nine types are admitted by the compiler; the rest render for reference but do nothing when the pipeline runs. The nine runtime admitted types | Category | Node types | See | | | | | | Interaction | Human in the loop (HITL), Printer | Interaction nodes | | Execution | LLM, Agent, Toolkit, MCP | Execution nodes | | Control flow | Decision, Router, State modifier | Control flow nodes | Deprecated node types The Add node menu only ever offers the nine types above — these older types can't be added to a new pipeline. If a pipeline built before this platform still has one, it renders read only on the canvas, but the compiler has no execution arm for it, so it doesn't run: Tool , Function , Pipeline , Condition , Loop , Loop from tool . If you're rebuilding a pipeline that still has one of these, replace it with the closest supported type: a Tool node becomes a Toolkit node, a Condition node becomes a Decision or Router node, and a Loop is restructured as a Router cycling back to an earlier node with an exit condition. There is no automatic migration — each one is a manual edit. A couple of other node shaped entries are sentinels rather than real node types: END marks where a path terminates (see Pipeline structure), and ghost /the default type are placeholders the editor uses internally. Two types that render but never run code and custom nodes can be added to a pipeline and configured in the flow editor, but the compiler has no execution arm for either one — they're accepted by the editor for future use, not by the runtime today. Don't build a pipeline that depends on one of these actually running; use an equivalent from the nine admitted types instead (a Toolkit node for custom logic that calls out to a service, for example).

title: Pipelines overview
text: A pipeline is a visual workflow: a sequence of connected nodes that execute in order, carrying a shared state between them. Where an agent has a single conversational loop, a pipeline lets you compose multiple steps — calling a toolkit, asking an LLM, branching on a decision, pausing for human approval — into one repeatable process. How a pipeline runs 1. Execution starts at the pipeline's designated entry point. 2. Each node performs its action and writes results into the pipeline's shared state. 3. The pipeline follows the connection from the current node to the next, based on the node's own routing (a plain edge, or a decision/router node's branch). 4. Execution ends when a transition reaches END . What a pipeline can use The flow editor's Add node menu only offers node types the runtime actually executes. Nine node types are admitted : decision , agent , toolkit , mcp , hitl , llm , printer , router , state modifier . Six older types — tool , pipeline , function , loop , loop from tool , condition — are deprecated: they still render if an older pipeline already contains them, but you cannot add new ones, and they carry a "Deprecated" badge in the editor. See Pipeline node types for the full comparison, and Pipeline structure for entry points, state and connections. For the full reference table, see Pipeline node reference. When to use a pipeline instead of an agent Reach for a pipeline when you need a defined, repeatable sequence of steps — gather input, call a toolkit, branch on the result, get human approval, produce an output — rather than an open ended conversation. Use an agent when the interaction should stay conversational and let the model decide what to do next. The two compose: a pipeline can include an agent node, and an agent can be attached to a chat conversation the same way a pipeline can. Guides and references Use the flow editor Pipeline structure: entry point, states and connections Pipeline node types View pipeline runs

title: View pipeline runs
text: When you run a pipeline, the flow editor shows progress directly on the canvas: nodes the run has reached pick up a status, and a run state indicator lets you open a step by step view of what happened. Run the pipeline (from its Configuration tab, or by using it in a conversation). As execution proceeds, nodes on the canvas update to show whether they're pending, running, done, or failed. Click the run state indicator to open a dialog with a stepper across every step the run has taken so far. Select a step to see the pipeline's state before and after it ran. From the same dialog, you can stop a run in progress. This page could not confirm from source whether a run's timeline stays inspectable after you navigate away and back, or only while the run view stays open — verify locally before relying on it for after the fact debugging. Run history The clock icon next to the run state indicator opens History : every past conversation that used this pipeline, newest first, with its date, a derived duration, and its message count. Select a run to see its recorded trace — the tool calls and thinking steps the runtime logged for that conversation. A pipeline with no past conversations shows an empty state rather than a blank panel. History has no "restore into the live test pane" action yet for pipelines — selecting a run opens its trace, but does not reload that conversation into the chat panel above (tracked in 868, the same partial restore gap agents' Configuration tab already discloses). Reading a step's state Each step in the timeline shows the pipeline's state as it was immediately before and immediately after that node ran. This is the most direct way to see what a Decision or Router node actually branched on, or what an LLM node's raw output was before a later node reshaped it — useful for working out why a pipeline took the path it did, or why it stopped where it did. A step that fails is marked with its own error status in the timeline, alongside the state at that point — checking the state there is usually the fastest way to tell whether the problem was bad input, a missing credential, or a node reading a state key that was never set. Guides and references Use the flow editor Pipeline structure: entry point, states and connections Pipeline node types

title: Pipeline structure: state, entry point and connections
text: A pipeline is a graph of nodes connected by transitions, with one starting point and one shared state object that every node can read and write. State: the pipeline's memory State is a structured object carried from node to node. Two states exist on every pipeline automatically: | State | Type | Holds | | | | | | input | string | The most recent user message | | messages | list | The full conversation history | Both are built in, but neither is reserved — you can read or write them like any other state key, and a new pipeline starts with them present but disabled until you turn them on for a node that needs them. Beyond those two, a pipeline has a fixed set of reserved keys the runtime manages itself — things like session id , thread id , output , result , hitl decisions , hitl interrupt , parallel tasks , and a family of internal resume markers. You can read them from a node, but avoid naming a custom state the same as one of these — the runtime will overwrite it with its own value. elitea hitl resume v1 , elitea tool resume v1 , elitea llm tool resume v1 , elitea pipeline node event scope v1 , elitea pipeline result trace v1 , elitea application task v1 , elitea application messages v1 , elitea application result v1 , elitea subgraph result v1 , output , result , router output , elitea response , printer output , state types , context info , hitl decisions , hitl interrupt , parallel tasks , pipeline blocked , session id , thread id , execution finished , chat history Add a custom state from the flow editor's States panel (next to the + button for adding nodes), or define it directly in YAML mode. Entry point Every pipeline has exactly one entry point — the node that runs first. Set it from a node's options menu ( Make entrypoint ), or in YAML with entry point: . A router node cannot be the entry point — it needs input from an earlier node to decide where to go. Setting a new entry point replaces the previous one; only one node holds it at a time. Node ports and connections Every node has one input port (top) and one output port (bottom). Most node types allow only a single outgoing connection; router and decision nodes are the exception — they can fan out to multiple targets, one of which is a labeled default/fallback path. Node names (ids) are restricted to letters, digits, , . , : and , up to 128 bytes. Ending a run END isn't a real node — it's a special connection target that stops execution. Drag a connector to the canvas and choose END , or set transition: END in YAML. Every path through the pipeline should eventually reach it; a path that never terminates can leave a run hanging.

title: Edit a pipeline as YAML
text: Alongside the flow editor, a pipeline's Configuration tab has a YAML view: a code editor over the same document the flow editor draws. A change in either view is reflected in the other — neither is a snapshot of the other. Schema Every pipeline document has three required top level sections: entry point names the node id execution starts from. state declares the pipeline's variables — each with a type and, optionally, a default value: input and messages are built in — the editor seeds them automatically and they don't need an initial value. Beyond those two, a state key cannot use one of the runtime's reserved names ( output , session id , chat history , and others the compiler uses internally) — see Pipeline structure for the full list. nodes is the array of node definitions — each entry names a node id (matching ^[A Za z0 9 .: ]+$ , at most 128 bytes) and a type from the nine the runtime admits. When to use YAML instead of Flow The YAML view is useful for copying a pipeline definition out for review or version control, editing many nodes at once, or working faster once you know the schema. For visually laying out nodes and connections, use the flow editor instead — the two views edit the same document, so switch freely. A minimal example This isn't a runnable pipeline on its own — it's meant to show the shape: an entry point, a state block, and a nodes array where each entry has an id and a type . A real pipeline also wires up each node's configuration (prompt, model, routing conditions), its connections to the next node, and a path into the reserved END sentinel to terminate — see Pipeline node types for why END isn't a node type you configure like the others. Guides and references Use the flow editor Pipeline structure: entry point, states and connections Pipeline node types

title: Elitea Docs
text: Elitea brings chat, agents, pipelines, toolkits, and platform administration into one workspace. These docs cover what the platform does today, how to set it up, and how to use each part of it. Concepts, the main menus, and personal and project settings. Install the platform and send your first chat message. Run the platform locally, on a local Kubernetes cluster, or the browser test stack. Task by task instructions for chat, pipelines, indexing, and more. Toolkits, MCP servers, and third party API access. Install and operate a production Kubernetes deployment with Helm and ArgoCD. Console for users, roles, authentication, budgets, and branding. Where to start New to Elitea? Read Overview of the Elitea platform, then Key concepts. Setting up a fresh deployment? Follow Install, then Configure an AI provider. Ready to chat? Go straight to Chat quick start. Connecting an external tool? See Connect toolkits quick start or the toolkit catalogue. Setting up a local development environment? Start at Set up a development environment. Deploying to production? Start at Production deployment overview, then Install with Helm. Administering a deployment? Start at Admin overview. Something not working? Check Troubleshooting or the FAQs.

title: Inventory
text: Inventory ingests one or more source repositories into a knowledge graph — files, functions, types and the relations between them — that you can filter, browse and ask questions of. Like Wikis, it lives at its own Inventory area, addressed by the Inventory toolkit that built the graph. Prerequisites An Inventory toolkit with at least one source added. A source toolkit of an allowed type — by default GitHub or ADO Repos (a deployment can widen this with ELITEA INVENTORY SOURCE TYPES ; GitLab and Bitbucket are not supported as sources even when connected as toolkits elsewhere). An llm model set on the Inventory toolkit — ingestion is refused without one. Build a knowledge graph If the project has none yet, add one — the Inventory area prompts you to when it finds none for the project. Under Sources , add a source toolkit (GitHub or ADO Repos, unless the deployment allows more) and its branch. Select Run ingestion . Progress shows per source: Pending, Ingesting…, Done, or Error. You can Stop ingestion on a source that's running. Browse the graph Filter entities by source, type and layer, and search by name. Select an entity to see its file location and its relations — incoming and outgoing edges to other entities. A source removed from the toolkit but still represented in the graph shows as "No longer configured — its entities are still in the graph," rather than disappearing silently. Ask about the inventory Select Ask this inventory to open a question panel over the graph. Answers name the entities they came from, rather than answering from general knowledge. Statistics and maintenance The Stats view breaks the graph down by layer and entity type, and reports cache size and cached graph count. Maintenance normalizes type name variations (for example "Feature" vs. "feature") and rebuilds the name, type, file and source indices. Common issues Inventory runs on the deployment's engine sidecar, not the Rust/Python agent worker — ingestion and browsing work the same regardless of which worker your deployment runs for agents and toolkits. "This toolkit configures no LLM model, so ingestion is refused" means you must set llm model in the Inventory toolkit's settings before Run ingestion will do anything. If the ingestion status can't be read, the per source states shown are stale, not necessarily current — re check after a refresh rather than assuming a source is still Pending.

title: Wikis (DeepWiki)
text: DeepWiki turns a code repository — or a folder of files in an artifact bucket — into browsable documentation: a page tree, diagrams, and a chat you can ask questions of. It lives at its own Wikis area, addressed by the wiki toolkit that generated it, rather than under Toolkits. DeepWiki needs the deployment's engine image tag and ELITEA DEEPWIKI ENABLED . A deployment on the default image lists and reads existing wikis but refuses every generation request. Prerequisites A wiki toolkit pointed at a source: a Repository (via a GitHub, GitLab or ADO Repos toolkit you've already connected), an Artifact folder , or a Bucket . An llm model and embedding model set on the toolkit, or a project default for both — generation and wiki chat fall back to the project's default model when the toolkit sets none, and refuse outright if the project has none either. Generate a wiki If the project has none yet, add one — the Wikis area prompts you to when it finds none for the project. Under the toolkit's own settings, set the wiki source: a repository toolkit to clone, an artifact folder, or a bucket. Optionally set a folder prefix to scope a bucket or artifact source. Select Generate wiki . Choose a planner mode ( Agentic or Clustering ) and whether to Skip tests , then confirm. Generation can take several minutes and runs one at a time per slot — if all slots are busy, wait or stop another run first. Browse and edit Once generated, browse the page tree, open Edit page to hand correct a page (diagrams that fail to render offer a one click fix you can accept or discard), and use Delete wiki to remove generated pages. Ask about the wiki Select Ask about this repository to open the chat drawer. Every question and answer is saved server side as you go, so closing the drawer or reloading the page does not lose the conversation — reopening it picks the same session back up, and your next question still carries the earlier turns as context. Use the history icon in the drawer's header to see this toolkit's past conversations, resume one, or delete one you no longer need. Clear the conversation starts a fresh session rather than erasing the old one — the previous conversation stays in the history list. You can attach two kinds of context to a question: Wiki pages — pick pages already published in the wiki you're reading; the server resolves the content, so what you attach is always what the wiki actually says. Files from your own machine — the paperclip with a badge control next to it lets you attach small text files (Markdown, plain text, CSV, most source code) up to a few hundred KB each and five files per question. Their content is read in your browser and sent along with the question; nothing is uploaded to the wiki's own pages. Both stay attached across questions in the same session until you remove them. Common issues DeepWiki runs on the deployment's engine sidecar, not the Rust/Python agent worker — generation and wiki chat work the same regardless of which worker your deployment runs for agents and toolkits. "No embedding model is set" or "No llm model is set" warnings mean generation or chat will use the project's default model for that role — and refuse outright if the project has none.

title: Make toolkit tools available by MCP
text: Agents and pipelines reach MCP clients through a tag, but toolkit tools reach them through a per toolkit checkbox: Make tools available by MCP , in the toolkit editor's Tools section. Only the tools you've selected on a flagged toolkit are published; nothing is exposed by default. Expose a toolkit's tools Open an existing toolkit (or create one — see the toolkit's own page under Toolkits), and go to its Tools tab. Choose which of the toolkit's tools should be callable at all (the same selection agents and pipelines use). Check Make tools available by MCP . Elitea publishes one MCP tool per selected tool, named (for example github create issue ). Select Save . The client's next tools/list call picks up the change — reconnect the client if it caches the tool list for the session. How a call runs A tools/call for a published toolkit tool dispatches through the same run path chat uses — with idempotency and polling for the worker's result — not a stub. It still needs the toolkit's own prerequisites: the right worker for that toolkit type, and a working credential. Common issues This only controls MCP exposure — the toolkit still needs to work in ordinary use (the right worker, a valid credential) before its tools will succeed when an MCP client calls them; see the toolkit's own page for that.

title: Elitea MCP server
text: Elitea is itself an MCP server: any client that speaks the Model Context Protocol can call your tagged agents, pipelines and toolkit tools as MCP tools. The transport is streamable HTTP — a single POST endpoint that answers initialize , tools/list and tools/call . There is no SSE stream and no stdio server: a GET on the endpoint answers "The server does not offer an SSE stream at this endpoint." Prerequisites Your project's MCP endpoint: https:// /app/ /mcp . Find the project ID in the project switcher or in the address bar of the app. A personal access token. Send it as Authorization: Bearer . See Create a token. Membership in the project. The server authenticates every request as the token owner. A token owner who is not a member of gets 403 forbidden . At least one agent or pipeline tagged mcp , or a toolkit with tools marked "available by MCP" (see Make tools available by MCP). Otherwise tools/list returns an empty list. An empty list is a correct answer. MCP exposure on the deployment. An administrator can turn it off. Then every request gets 403 with "MCP exposure is disabled on this deployment". Create a token Go to Settings → Personal tokens ( /settings/tokens ). Click + . Give the token a name, for example mcp claude code . Set an expiration date. Click Generate . Copy the value immediately. The dialog shows it only once. For more detail, see Create a personal access token. The token gives the same access as your account. Do not commit a client configuration file that contains the token. Use one token for each client, so that you can revoke one client without the others. Tag an agent or pipeline for MCP Open the agent or pipeline you want to expose. Add the tag mcp to it. Elitea exposes one tool per tagged agent/pipeline, taking a single free form task string as input. If the agent has several tagged versions, the newest tagged one is the one served — not necessarily the version marked "latest" in the UI. Retag or delete older tagged versions if you need a specific one served. Connect a client The server speaks the streamable HTTP transport only. Every client below sends POST requests to the endpoint with a static Authorization header. Run this command once: Add scope user to make the server available in all your projects. Run claude mcp list to make sure that the server connects. In a session, type /mcp to see the Elitea tools. Add a server entry to .cursor/mcp.json (project) or ~/.cursor/mcp.json (global): Open Cursor Settings → MCP and make sure that the elitea server shows a green status and its tools. Add a server entry to .vscode/mcp.json (workspace) or your user mcp.json (global): Reload the MCP server list. Then select tools from your Elitea project in Copilot Chat's Agent mode. Claude Desktop custom connectors do not send a static Authorization header. Use the mcp remote bridge. The bridge runs locally, adds the header, and forwards each request to Elitea. It needs Node.js 18 or later. Open Settings → Developer → Edit Config . Add this entry to claude desktop config.json : Restart Claude Desktop. The header value is in env because some platforms split an argument that contains a space. transport http only stops the bridge from a retry with the older SSE transport, which this server does not support. Common issues A toolkit tool called through this MCP server runs on the platform's agent worker, under the toolkit's own credential, like a Test tools run from the toolkit editor. Agent and pipeline tools tagged mcp run the same way as in chat. Two agents that sanitize to the same tool name collapse into one entry in tools/list — whichever the database returns first wins, silently. Give MCP tagged agents and pipelines unique names. The endpoint accepts POST only. A client that opens a GET (SSE) connection gets 405 with "The server does not offer an SSE stream at this endpoint". A client that supports only the older SSE transport cannot connect. Use a client that speaks streamable HTTP. | Response | Cause | Action | | | | | | 401 unauthorized | The token is missing, expired or revoked. | Create a new token and update the client configuration. | | 403 forbidden | The token owner is not a member of the project. | Ask a project administrator to add you, or use a project ID that you are a member of. | | 403 "MCP exposure is disabled on this deployment" | An administrator turned off MCP exposure. | Ask the administrator to turn it on. | | 405 "The server does not offer an SSE stream at this endpoint" | The client sent GET to open an SSE stream. | Configure the client for the HTTP transport, not SSE. | | Empty tools/list | No agent or pipeline has the mcp tag, and no toolkit tool is available by MCP. | Add the mcp tag, as in Tag an agent or pipeline for MCP. |

title: Pre-built MCP servers
text: An admin can curate a catalogue of MCP servers that every project sees as ready made toolkit tiles, so project members don't each have to look up a URL and register their own OAuth client. This replaces what the legacy docs called "EPAM MCPs" — the mechanism is now vendor neutral; an admin can add any MCP server here, not a fixed list. Add a server to the catalogue As an admin, open Configuration in the admin console and go to the MCP servers section. Select Add MCP server . Give it a display name (its catalogue key is derived from the name, or fixed once other projects reference it) and the server's base URL. If the server needs OAuth and doesn't support Dynamic Client Registration, enter the OAuth client ID and client secret . The secret is sealed into the platform vault immediately — no endpoint ever returns it again, including this form on a later edit. Check Offer this server to projects , then Save . Project members now see it as a tile, the same as a hand added Remote MCP. Common issues A catalogued server is a built in Elitea type, not part of the toolkit catalogue. Only HTTP based servers can be catalogued in the first place, and that is the only transport the worker's MCP client needs. Removing a catalogued server deletes its stored client secret permanently. To stop offering a server without losing the secret, edit it and clear Offer this server to projects instead of deleting it. Stdio transport MCP servers are refused here — only HTTP based remote servers can be catalogued.

title: Remote MCP
text: Remote MCP is the other direction from the Elitea MCP server: instead of exposing Elitea's tools to an external client, a Remote MCP toolkit lets an Elitea agent or pipeline call tools hosted on someone else's MCP server. It's listed as Remote MCP in the toolkit type picker; there is no local or stdio MCP client — only this HTTP connection. Prerequisites The remote server's URL. If the server requires OAuth: either nothing further (if it supports Dynamic Client Registration) or a pre registered OAuth client ID and secret from that server's own admin console. Connect a remote MCP server In the left navigation, open Toolkits , then select New , and choose Remote MCP . Enter the remote server's streamable HTTP endpoint (usually ending in /mcp ) and save. A same origin redirect, such as /mcp to /mcp/ , is followed; a redirect to another host is not. If the server requires OAuth, Elitea opens an authorization dialog — automatically, either now or the first time an agent tries to call one of its tools. Servers that support Dynamic Client Registration need nothing from you beyond clicking Authorize ; a server that doesn't asks for a Client ID and Client Secret first. The flow uses PKCE or OIDC depending on what the server advertises, and you can choose to remember the credentials for the session. Once authorized, Elitea calls the remote server's tools/list and shows the tools it offers. Attach the toolkit to an agent or pipeline the same way as any other toolkit. Common issues Remote MCP is a built in Elitea type, not part of the toolkit catalogue. The worker's MCP client speaks streamable HTTP, which is the only transport a remote server can use here anyway. The deprecated HTTP+SSE transport is not supported. A URL ending in /sse that the server refuses (many providers have retired these endpoints) fails with a message naming the endpoint and suggesting its /mcp replacement; point the toolkit at that /mcp URL instead. If you set an Authorization header (for example a personal access token) on the toolkit, it is used both when you load tools and when an agent runs, even if you have also authorized the server through the dialog. Remove the header to use the OAuth authorization instead. With caching enabled, the tool list is reused for Cache TTL seconds (60 to 3600, default 300) before the server is asked again. Each run still opens its own connection with its own credentials; only the list of tools is reused. When an agent first calls one of that server's tools in a run, the worker lists the tools on that run's connection once, so the call behaves exactly as an uncached one. Authorization can happen mid conversation: if a tool call fails because the session isn't authorized yet, Elitea shows the same authorization dialog from chat. Send your message again once it succeeds. The redirect for the OAuth flow lands on /mcp auth callback . If you're testing behind a proxy or a non default host, make sure that path is reachable at the same origin the browser used to start the flow.

title: API usage
text: Everything the web app does goes through the same REST API you can call directly — from a script, a Power Automate flow, or any HTTP client that can send a bearer token. Authenticate Open Settings › Personal tokens and create a token. Copy it immediately — it's shown once. Add an Authorization: Bearer header. A legacy compatibility alternative, X API Key: , is also accepted. Most endpoints take a project id in the path. A token can only act on projects its owner belongs to. Endpoint layout REST endpoints live under /api/v2/... — the same paths the web app calls. Interactive API documentation (OpenAPI/Swagger UI) is served at /api/docs , with the raw spec at /api/openapi.yaml and /api/openapi.json . Both are public — no token needed to read the spec. The MCP server is at /app/{projectID}/mcp (see Elitea MCP server) — the same bearer token authenticates it. SCIM provisioning, for identity providers that push users and groups, is at /api/v2/scim/v2 . It authenticates with a dedicated SCIM client credential that you create under Authentication; a personal access token is refused. Call the API from Power Automate (or any HTTP client) In your flow, add a generic HTTP (or "HTTP with Azure AD" if you prefer a service account) action. Point it at the /api/v2/... path for the operation you need — check /api/docs for the exact path, parameters and body shape. Set the header to Bearer , stored as a secret in your flow, not inline in plain text. Common issues A token only reaches projects its owner belongs to — a 403 on an otherwise correct call usually means the token owner isn't a member of the project id in the path, not a malformed request. Webhooks (both directions) have a UI now: a pipeline's inbound trigger is configured from the pipeline editor's Triggers & schedules panel, and the project's outbound webhook registry has its own Settings › Webhooks page — see Webhooks and pipeline triggers. Both APIs still work with a personal access token if you'd rather script registration.

title: ADO boards
text: Read and manage Azure DevOps boards: work items, queries and area/iteration paths. It's listed under the project management category in the toolkit type picker. Prerequisites An account at ADO boards with permission to issue an API token or credential, saved in Elitea as a ado credential ( /credentials/create credential/ ). Or skip the saved credential and paste token directly into the toolkit's own settings (inline auth). If you plan to index content for retrieval: an embedding model, configured under AI providers. Connect the toolkit In the left navigation, open Toolkits , then select New . Filter the type picker by the project management category, or search for "ADO boards". Under the credential field, choose an existing ado credential, or select Create credential to add one without leaving the form. If you plan to index this source, set an embedding model . Indexes are kept in the platform's vector store, so there is no vector storage setting to pick. Leave it empty to use the toolkit without indexing. Name the toolkit and select Create . It's now available to attach to agents, pipelines and conversations in this project. Available tools | Tool | | | | Attach file to work item | | Create work item | | Delete work item | | Get comments | | Get image by url | | Get relation types | | Get work item | | Get work item type fields | | Index data | | Link work items | | Link work items to wiki page | | List indexes | | Remove index | | Search index | | Search work items | | Stepback search index | | Stepback summary index | | Unlink work items from wiki page | | Update work item | Common issues The Indexes tab only appears when the configured worker can run this type's index data tool; if the worker can't, the tab is hidden and shows the worker's refusal message. index data itself can't be run from the Test tools pane — use the Indexes tab. The credential form for ADO boards supports Check connection — use it before saving to confirm Elitea can reach ADO boards with these details, instead of discovering an auth problem from a failed tool call later.

title: ADO repos
text: Read and write files, branches and pull requests in an Azure DevOps Git repository. It's listed under the code repositories category in the toolkit type picker. Prerequisites An account at ADO repos with permission to issue an API token or credential, saved in Elitea as a ado credential ( /credentials/create credential/ ). Or skip the saved credential and paste token directly into the toolkit's own settings (inline auth). If you plan to index content for retrieval: an embedding model, configured under AI providers. Connect the toolkit In the left navigation, open Toolkits , then select New . Filter the type picker by the code repositories category, or search for "ADO repos". Under the credential field, choose an existing ado credential, or select Create credential to add one without leaving the form. If you plan to index this source, set an embedding model . title: Custom
text: Custom isn't a vendor integration — it's a fallback editor. Every toolkit type normally gets a typed form built from its schema, but Custom always appears at the bottom of the type picker as a generic JSON settings editor you can point at any type. Use it when a type has no typed form yet, or when you need to set a field the form doesn't expose. Custom is added by the web client itself and has no entry in the toolkit type catalogue — there's no fixed tool list or worker verdict to report, because it isn't a type on its own. It edits the settings of whatever underlying toolkit type you choose. Prerequisites The toolkit type key you want to configure (for example github or jira ) and the field names its schema expects — check that type's own page in this catalogue, or the type's settings in the create form first. Any credential the underlying type needs, created the normal way under Credentials. Configure a toolkit as raw JSON In the left navigation, open Toolkits , then select New . Custom is listed at the end of the type picker, outside the category filters. The editor is a JSON text area with syntax highlighting and linting. Enter the type and settings fields the underlying toolkit type expects. Name the toolkit and select Create . Elitea validates the JSON but does not re check it against the target type's schema beyond basic parsing — a field name typo won't be caught here. Available tools There's no fixed tool list — the tools exposed are whatever the underlying toolkit type provides once its settings are valid. Common issues A malformed or incomplete settings object saves without error but fails at call time, not at save time. Prefer the type's own dedicated form when one is available, and reach for Custom only for the fields it's missing.

title: Memory
text: The Memory toolkit gives an agent, pipeline or conversation a small key value store it can write to and search across turns — separate from the conversation's own chat history. It's listed under the other category in the toolkit type picker. This is a different feature from Settings › Memory's Long term Memory section, which recalls facts about you automatically, before a turn starts, across every conversation — with no tool call involved. The Memory toolkit here is a real, attachable tool the model calls itself, mid turn, against its own key value store. Prerequisites No credential: the form does not ask for one, and memories are kept in the platform's vector store. An administrator must have turned on indexing, with the vector store, and set the memory embedding model ( worker.runtime.memoryEmbeddingModel ); without it the Memory type is hidden from the picker with that reason. No vendor account is needed — the store lives inside your project. Connect the toolkit In the left navigation, open Toolkits , then select New . Filter the type picker by the other category, or search for "Memory". Name the toolkit and select Create . Attach it to an agent, pipeline or conversation the same way as any other toolkit. Available tools | Tool | | | | Delete memory | | Get memory | | Manage memory | | Search memory | Common issues Memories are stored in the platform's vector store, scoped to your project and to the toolkit itself (the Namespace is only a label inside the toolkit, so two toolkits never share memories even with the same namespace), and search memory ranks them by how close they are to the query. Memories saved under the retired Python worker (rows in a pgvector database) were not carried over. A memory holds up to 16 KiB of content and 8 KiB of metadata, a key is at most 256 bytes, and a namespace holds up to 10,000 memories and versions; search memory returns at most 50 results. Memory scope . Personal (the default): each person has a private memory, and nobody else can read, search or delete it. Project : one memory shared by everyone in the project. Both : the agent chooses per memory, personal unless it says project. Anything saved to project memory is read back by every later conversation in the project as a fact, so in Both mode the agent is told to save there only when the person asked and never to copy personal memories or text that came from a web page, a document or a tool. If an agent reads untrusted content, prefer Personal only. A scheduled run acts as the person who owns the schedule and uses that person's personal memory. Personal memory is available only in a private conversation that only you are in; in a shared or public conversation, or in a toolkit run outside a conversation, the agent says so and project memory still works. This is checked on every call. Memories are kept per project, and the platform, not the agent, keeps one person's personal memory from another: it is enforced where the memories are stored. Saving to an existing key keeps the old value as history instead of overwriting it. get memory and search memory return the current value; they also accept as of (an RFC 3339 timestamp, to see what was true then) and include history . delete memory removes every version. A key keeps at most 20 versions. Deleting the toolkit deletes all of its memories, including every person's personal ones; a person who leaves the project, or is deleted, has their personal memories deleted too (retried until it succeeds). The store is scoped to whatever key you give it — an agent must be instructed (or coded, in a pipeline) to use consistent keys, or writes and reads won't line up. There is no automatic per user or per conversation partitioning.

title: Web Search and Host Intelligence
text: Two toolkit types let an agent reach the public internet. Both run on the Rust worker and are read only. Web Search ( web ): web search and web fetch . web fetch reads a page through the platform's egress guard, which refuses private and metadata addresses and checks every redirect, or through a provider's extract API. Host Intelligence ( host intel ): internet host search and internet host lookup , through Shodan. It is off until a platform administrator grants it to a project in Admin › Toolkits . Every call is admitted by the same budget engine as model calls before the provider is called, and billed afterwards. Tool spend appears in Settings › Usage as rows such as "Web search · Tavily", next to the model rows, and in run analytics. When a project or member budget runs out, the tool is refused with the same message and Usage link as a refused model call, and the provider isn't called. Set up a provider In Admin › Configuration › Web search , add the provider to Enabled providers . A configured key alone doesn't turn a provider on. The same section sets the default search provider, whether direct fetch is allowed, the fetch allow and deny domain lists, and the result caps. Create a tavily , firecrawl , brave search , duckduckgo instant or shodan credential. A project uses its own credential first. If it has none, it uses a shared credential in the public project, except for Shodan, which only accepts a project's own key. Open Admin › LLM proxy › Tools . Each operation has a price per request, credit or page. An operation without a price is refused, and free operations have an explicit $0. Change the price if your plan differs from the default. Create a Web Search or Host Intelligence toolkit and attach it to an agent. On the desktop, the native client policy must also allow it ( local work.web , local work.host intel , both off by default). Providers Prices, limits and terms change, so check them with the provider before you rely on them. Hobby $19/month for 5,000 credits, up to Scale $599/month for 1M | $5 per 1,000 search requests | Free | Query credits: Freelancer $69/month for 10,000 (about $0.0069 each), Small Business $359/month for 200,000 | | Default price | $0.008 per credit | $0.0038 per credit or page | $0.005 per request | $0 | $0.0069 per credit | | Free tier | 1,000 credits a month, no card | 1,000 credits a month, no card | $5 of credits a month (about 1,000 searches), card required | Free, no published quota | A free API plan, but most methods need at least Membership ($49 once). title: Agents
text: An agent combines instructions, a model, and optional toolkits and skills into a reusable assistant. This page covers the Agents menu end to end; for the underlying concept, see What is an agent. Create an agent Select + Agent in the sidebar. Name and Description are required; Instructions define the agent's behavior. Tags, a welcome message, and up to four conversation starters are optional. Saving creates the agent's first ("latest") version and opens its full configuration page: a form on the left, a live test chat on the right. Select Build with AI on a new agent, or Edit with AI on a saved one, to describe what you want in plain language and review a generated draft — name, description, instructions, welcome message, starters, and suggested toolkits — before applying it. Attach toolkits, agents, MCPs, and pipelines In the Tools section, use the +Toolkit , +MCP , +Agent , and +Pipeline buttons to attach existing resources; each opens a searchable picker with a Create new option that takes you to that resource's own creation form. Changes save automatically. If an attached toolkit uses shared credentials that require your own private copy, a Credential setup required banner appears on its card — select Create a credential to add the matching private credential. Skills Attach up to five skills per agent version from the Skills section. Each attached skill uses its base version by default; select the version name on the card to switch to a different one. The Skills section is hidden when the Public project is selected. Modules Built in modules — attachments, image creation, data analysis, planner, smart tools selection, swarm mode, and the platform's own MCP tools — turn on in Tools › Modules . Image creation, swarm mode and the platform's MCP tools show disabled with a reason: the platform's worker does not run them. See Internal tools. Instructions, variables, and mentions Type / in Instructions to mention a toolkit, MCP, agent, or pipeline already attached to the agent, and ~ to mention an attached skill. A {{variable name}} placeholder in Instructions automatically adds a matching input field to the Variables section. Editor notes A free text Editor Notes field records internal context about the current version — it is never sent to the model or used during execution. Test the agent The embedded chat panel on the right lets you send messages, pick a model and its settings (Reasoning for reasoning models, Creativity for standard ones, Max Completion Tokens), and iterate without leaving the page. When context management is on for the project, a Context Budget widget appears above the panel after the first message. Versions Selecting Save again updates the current version. Use Save As Version to branch off a named version instead — version names must be 48 characters or fewer, without spaces or underscores. From any version you can Delete , Execute , or switch versions from the version dropdown. See Entity versioning. Publish, export, import, and fork Publish a draft version through a guided wizard with automated AI validation, making it visible in Catalog. See Agent publishing. Export downloads the selected version as a single .md file, or a .zip if it references nested agents. Import an exported file from the Agents dashboard toolbar. Fork copies the selected version into another project you choose. See Import/export and Forking for full detail; toolkit credentials must be reconfigured manually after either operation. Evaluation A saved agent's editor includes an Evaluation tab to define what "good" looks like for that agent, run it against test cases, and see how it scored. Define scoring dimensions — the criteria a run is judged against, such as accuracy or tone — building up a reusable set of judging criteria before running anything. Create a dataset of test cases: inputs paired with what you expect the agent to do with them. A run executes against a dataset. Start a run against a dataset and your dimensions. Runs poll for progress while this tab stays open — leaving it pauses polling until you return — and produce a scorecard with one score per dimension per case when they finish. History A saved agent's editor also includes a History tab: every past conversation that used this agent, newest first, with its date, a derived duration, and its message count. Select a run to see its recorded trace — the tool calls and thinking steps the runtime logged for that conversation. An agent with no past conversations shows an empty state rather than a blank panel. Selecting a run in History does not currently reload that conversation into the Test panel above — there is no live restore path from this tab (issue 868, same disclosed gap as pipelines' equivalent History tab). Best practices Be specific about the agent's goal, scope, and constraints; give examples where useful. Attach only the toolkits and tools the agent actually needs. Branch a version before a change you might need to roll back from. Run the agent through its conversation starters and a few edge cases before you publish it. Troubleshooting Check the selected model and its settings, and confirm any attached toolkits are configured correctly. Confirm you have publishing permission and that all required fields are complete; review the AI validation result for blocking issues. Save the agent first — Skills can only be attached to a saved version — or check whether the five skill limit has been reached. Skills · Toolkits · Project Context · Sensitive action authorization guardrail · Build agent with AI

title: Applications
text: Applications are complete, focused solutions — not general purpose toolkits — that open their own interface inside Elitea once configured. Today's catalogue has two: DeepWiki (wikis) and Inventory. See DeepWiki and Inventory for what each one does. Applications and App Catalog tabs The Applications tab lists instances already configured in the current project, in card or table view, filterable by type and pinnable for quick access. The App Catalog tab shows every application type available on the platform, each tagged Available , Configured , or By request . Configure an application Open App Catalog and find the application you want. Select Configure — shown only when your project already has access. For DeepWiki: a code toolkit, an LLM model, a max token budget, and an embedding model. For Inventory: one or more repository toolkits and the AI model settings. Select Save . The new instance appears on the Applications tab; open it to reach its interface. Request access If a catalog card shows By request , select Request Access , describe your use case, and submit. The card then shows Pending approval until an administrator reviews the request through App requests. Troubleshooting Your project has not been granted access to that application type yet — submit a request first. Confirm its underlying toolkit (the repository toolkit for DeepWiki or Inventory) still has valid credentials. DeepWiki and Inventory · Toolkits

title: Artifacts
text: Artifacts are project scoped, bucket organized file storage that agents, pipelines, and conversations read from and write to. Chat attachments and generated images land here automatically in a default attachments bucket; you can also create buckets of your own. Create a bucket 1. Select + Create Bucket . 2. Enter a Name (starts with a letter; letters, numbers, and hyphens only; 56 characters max). 3. Select Save . Creating a bucket does not set a retention period — that is configured separately, after the bucket exists. Retention Open a bucket's edit view to set a retention period in whole days. Leave it empty to keep files indefinitely; set it and files older than that many days become eligible for automatic deletion, which cannot be undone. Upload, preview, and manage files Upload by dragging files onto the file table, using the upload button, or from a bucket's context menu. Select a file's view/edit icon to preview it — code, Markdown, MDX, CSV/TSV, Mermaid, images, and DOCX all render with type appropriate views, and most can be edited in place and saved back (files over 2 MB cannot be previewed or edited). A text like file's preview also offers Open in canvas , which opens it in the richer Canvas editor — syntax highlighting, a table grid, or a Mermaid live preview — and can save the edit back to the same file. Download a single file or select several and download them together as a ZIP. Deleting all files in a folder removes the folder too — empty folders are not supported. Editing an artifact file is last save wins. If two people edit the same file at once, the later save overwrites the earlier one. Manage bucket access In team and public projects, open a bucket's Manage permissions action to set per user exceptions to the default read/write access: Read only or No access for one or more users. Selecting the default read/write option in an edit removes the exception. This is not available in personal projects. Retention notifications When a bucket's retention period is about to delete files, the bucket's owner gets a notification 24 hours ahead so there is time to back up anything still needed. See Notifications. Use a bucket from an agent or pipeline Attach the built in Artifact toolkit type to an agent or pipeline to let it read and write files in a bucket during a run — useful for a workflow that produces a report, or one that reads reference material uploaded ahead of time. An Artifact toolkit is also index capable, so an agent can search across everything in a bucket instead of reading one file at a time. See Indexing overview. Troubleshooting Confirm a bucket or folder is selected and that you hold the artifacts create permission. Check the name follows the naming rules — it must start with a letter and use only letters, numbers, and hyphens. Its bucket's retention period may have expired, or another user or an agent with Artifact toolkit access may have removed it — check the bucket's retention setting and project activity. Attach files · Data analysis · Notifications

title: Catalog
text: Catalog is the shared library of published agents and skills, visible across every project you have access to — a discovery surface, not a personal workspace. Reach it from the Catalog button near the bottom of the sidebar. Agents and Skills tabs Agents — published agents shown as cards with creator, likes, and a Start chat action. Select a card to view its full description, instructions (read only), welcome message, and conversation starters. Skills — published skills you can review and attach to one or more of your own agents with Add or Add & Test (the latter also opens a chat with the agent you attached it to). Filter either tab by category (Trending, My liked, Development, DevOps, and more) or search by name and description. Start a conversation from Catalog Select Start chat on an agent, or one of its conversation starters, to create a new conversation with that agent already active and its participant added. What you can and cannot change Published items are read only. In a conversation with a published agent you can change the model , its settings (Creativity or Reasoning Effort, Max Completion Tokens, Steps Limit), and the values of any variables it defines — these changes apply only to your conversation. You cannot edit its name, instructions, welcome message, conversation starters, or attached toolkits; to get an editable copy, fork it or build your own from the Agents menu. Troubleshooting It may not be published yet, still pending moderation, or filtered out by an active search or category filter. Refresh the page and confirm you still have Chat access; if the problem persists, contact your administrator. Agents · Skills · Use public items from chat · Agent publishing

title: Chat
text: Chat is the central place where Elitea's capabilities come together. Each conversation is an independent session — you can reference earlier messages in the same conversation, but context is not shared between separate conversations. Conversations are stored on the server and accessible from any device. Create a conversation 1. Go to Chat in the sidebar. 2. Select + Conversation , or start typing in the welcome screen's input. 3. Optionally add participants first — select + in the input toolbar, or type to search. 4. Type your message and send it. The conversation name is generated automatically from the message content. Unsent messages What you type but do not send stays with its conversation. Switch to another conversation, another project or a Local work thread, and when you come back the text is in the input for you to finish. A new chat keeps its own unsent text per project until you send it. Unsent text is kept on this device only (desktop app, browser or mobile app) and is cleared when you sign out. Conversations in the sidebar are grouped by Today , Yesterday , This Week , and Older ; pinned conversations always sit at the top. Folders Select the folder icon in the conversations header to create a folder, then drag conversations into it or use Move to from a conversation's context menu. In a personal project, folders and their contents are visible only to you. In a team project, folders can be shared with the whole project and cannot be converted back to private. Participants Participants extend what a conversation can do: A language model you talk to directly. Existing agents or pipelines from your project or the public catalog. Integrations already configured in the project, targetable directly with / . Connected MCP servers that expose additional tools. In team projects, teammates you can mention with @username . To add a participant, select + in the input toolbar and browse by category, or type followed by a name to search across agents, pipelines, toolkits, and MCPs. Added participants appear in the Participants panel on the right, grouped by type; select an agent or pipeline card to make it the active participant. Hovering an existing participant's card reveals an edit icon that opens its inline editor (the same form as its own menu page) without leaving the conversation. Each category (Agents, Pipelines, Toolkits, and the MCPs category's own view) also offers a Create new row above the existing item list. Selecting it opens the same inline editor a participant's own edit icon opens, in create mode; saving creates the agent/pipeline/toolkit and attaches it to the current conversation as a participant, the same as picking an existing one. See Edit agents, pipelines, toolkits and MCPs from chat. Mention a toolkit or tool Type / to search toolkits and MCPs already added to the conversation, then / again after a toolkit name to filter its individual tools. The result is inserted as /ToolkitName/ToolName , directing the AI to use that specific tool. Modules Chat supports several built in modules — image creation, data analysis, planner, smart tools selection, swarm mode, and the platform's own MCP tools — turned on from + → Modules . Image creation, swarm mode and the platform's MCP tools show disabled with a reason: the platform's worker does not run them. See Internal tools for what each one does. File attachments Select + → Attach Files , drag files onto the input, or paste from the clipboard. Images go straight to the model for visual analysis; other files are indexed and retrieved by semantic search. Files land in the project's default attachments artifact bucket automatically — no manual toolkit setup is required. Direct model chats always allow attachments; an agent or pipeline needs attachments turned on in its own configuration first. Choose a model and settings Select the model chip at the bottom of the chat to pick a model, and the settings gear next to it to adjust generation parameters. In the desktop app the model shows as its name with a ⌄ , and the settings are under ⋯ → Model settings… , with Read replies aloud , Voice settings… and Clear chat history… . Drag the top edge of the input to make it taller or shorter; the app remembers the height. Reasoning capable models expose a Reasoning level (Low/Medium/High); standard models expose Creativity (1–5). All models let you set Max Completion Tokens (Auto or a custom value), and conversations additionally expose a Steps Limit capping how many tool calls a turn can make (default 25). Reply actions The conversation reads like a chat: your own messages sit on the right in a tinted bubble, other people's on the left under their name, and replies sit on the left in a neutral bubble, named only when more than one agent answers in the conversation. Chat and Local work threads share one centred reading column, the message box included. Under each reply is one row of actions: Copy , Good and Bad (with a comment once you vote), Read out , Regenerate , and ⋯ for Remember this , Open as document , Fork from here and Delete . The row always shows under the latest reply; under older replies it appears when you point at the reply or tab to it. Your own messages get the same kind of row, with Copy , Edit , Fork and Delete , shown when you point at the message. Each row ends with when the message was sent, and a reply that drew on your saved memories also shows Using N memories there. If the model thought before answering, a Thought for … line sits above the reply. It stays folded while the model works and after it answers; click it to see the steps. Stop a reply and queue messages The message box stays open while a reply is written. What you send then waits in the Queued list at the top of the message box: the agent reads it at its next step, or it goes as the next message once the reply ends. Each queued message has Send now (stop the reply and send this message first), Edit (take it back into the message box) and Remove . With nothing typed, the button at the end of the message box is Stop ; you can also press Esc twice quickly anywhere on the page. After a Stop, the app asks before it sends the messages the agent had not read yet. Voice Dictate into the input; transcribed text lands at the cursor. Have a response read aloud from a mini player in the input area. A hands free loop: record, send, listen to the reply, record again. Voice input uses a server side speech recognition model when your project has one configured (Settings › AI Providers), falling back to the browser's Web Speech API; text to speech works the same way with a server TTS model or the browser's speech synthesis as a fallback. Voice settings (voice, speed, volume) are saved per browser and can also be set as your default in Settings › Personal Settings. Context budget When context management is turned on for the project (Settings › Memory), a Context Budget panel appears at the foot of the participants panel (the only place it is shown) after your first message, showing token usage and letting you trigger manual pruning or review the active summarization settings. Share a conversation Open a conversation's context menu and select Share by link to open the share dialog. Choose a link expiry (1 hour, 1 day, 7 days, or 30 days — there is no non expiring option) and, optionally, a password of at least 8 characters. The link is shown once, at creation, and copied to your clipboard automatically; it cannot be retrieved again later — if you lose it, revoke it and create a new one. Anyone who opens the link sees the conversation as it stood at share time in a read only, anonymous viewer — they can reply to nothing and add no participants — prompted for the password first if one was set. An invalid, revoked, or expired link all show the same "unavailable" message by design, so a visitor cannot tell which case applies. Sensitive action authorization When an agent or pipeline is about to call a tool your administrator has marked sensitive, the conversation pauses and shows an authorization card with the action and its parameters (secrets masked) before anything executes. See Sensitive action authorization guardrail. Canvas When a response contains code, a table, a Mermaid diagram, or prose, a pencil icon (or, for a whole prose reply, the Open as document icon in the answer's action row) opens it in Canvas for direct, real time collaborative editing — prose opens in a rich text document editor with headings, lists, bold/italic/code, links, and basic tables, backed by Markdown. Canvas can also open a previously stored text like file — from a message attachment's own toolbar, or from a bucket file in Artifacts — and save its document back to the artifact store under a bucket and filename you choose. See How to use Canvas. Troubleshooting Confirm the agent, pipeline, toolkit, or MCP exists and is accessible to you in the current project. Attachments are always on for a direct model chat, but need to be turned on in the agent's or pipeline's own configuration first. No server side voice model is configured and your browser does not support the Web Speech API. Ask your administrator to configure one in AI Providers. The link may be expired, revoked, or never valid — Elitea shows the same message in every case to avoid confirming which. Attach files · Context management · Add teammates to a conversation

title: Credentials
text: A credential holds the authentication information — API key, token, username/password, or similar — a toolkit or AI provider needs to connect to an external service. Storing credentials centrally means you configure them once and reuse them across multiple toolkits and agents. Create a credential Select + Create from the Credentials page. Choose a credential type from the categorized list (code repositories, project management, testing, and more — matching the toolkit catalogue). Enter Display Name , a unique ID , and the type's specific fields — a URL, a username, and a key or token. Where offered, select Test Connection to verify the values before saving. Select Save . When a field accepts a secret, use Settings › Secrets instead of typing the value directly — the field's dropdown lets you create a new project or private secret inline. Project vs. private credentials A credential can be shared with the team (visible to any project member configuring a toolkit) or kept private to you. Team shared toolkits sometimes require each member to hold a matching private credential — see the shared credential note on the Toolkits page. Edit or delete a credential Open a credential from the dashboard to update its name or parameters and select Save , or use the delete action and confirm by typing its name. Deleting a credential in use will break the toolkit or agent that depends on it. Assign a credential When creating or editing a toolkit or an AI provider configuration, open its Credentials dropdown and select an existing credential, or create one inline. Troubleshooting Check that the key, token, or password is correct, current, and free of stray whitespace, and that your account still has access to the target service. Confirm you are viewing the right project, and that the credential has not been deleted by another team member. How to use credentials · Toolkits · Secrets

title: DeepWiki and Inventory
text: DeepWiki and Inventory are configured from Applications and, once set up, open at /deepwiki and /inventory . Visiting either route resolves your project's configured toolkit automatically: it opens directly if there is exactly one, offers a picker if there are several, or shows an empty state if none is configured yet.
